1.1.title: What is a differential equation?
goals: Verify a proposed solution and its initial data
1.1.trap: Linearity concerns y and its derivatives, not the independent variable.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does y(0)=1 alone prove that y=eᵗ solves y′=2y?
hints: Check the derivative as well as the initial value.
steps: No. An initial value checks only one point. For eᵗ the derivative is eᵗ while the right side is 2eᵗ, so the differential equation fails.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why is t²y′+cos(t)y=t linear while y′+y²=t is nonlinear?
hints: Ask which variable is being squared.
steps: Coefficients may depend on t. The first equation is linear in y and y′; the second squares the unknown, which breaks linearity.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Classify an equation
problems.prompt: Give an example of a third-order linear ODE and explain its classification.
hints: Use y and its derivatives only to the first power.
steps: Choose \(y^{(3)}+t^2y\prime+\sin(t)y=e^t\).
The highest derivative is the third derivative. All coefficients depend only on t.
problems.check: A product such as yy′ would make it nonlinear.

problems.title: Verify by substitution
problems.prompt: Check that \(y=1-t^2\) solves \(ty\prime-y=-(1+t^2)\).
hints: Differentiate first; then substitute both y and y′.
steps: \(y\prime=-2t\).
problems.check: The left and right sides agree identically.

problems.title: A cycle of derivatives
hints: The derivatives repeat every four steps.
steps: From the ODE, \(y^{(k+2)}=-y^{(k)}\).
The values start 1, 0, −1, 0, and repeat.
problems.check: The formula gives 1 at k=0 and 0 at k=1.

problems.title: Classify, then verify
problems.prompt: Classify \(y''-3y'+2y=0\) and verify y=e²ᵗ. Does it satisfy y(0)=1,y′(0)=2?
hints: Compute both derivatives.
steps: The equation has order 2 and is linear homogeneous. For y=e²ᵗ, y′=2e²ᵗ and y″=4e²ᵗ.
Substitution gives (4−6+2)e²ᵗ=0. The values at 0 are 1 and 2.
problems.answer: y=e^{2t}\text{ satisfies the ODE and data.}
problems.check: The equation and both initial conditions were checked independently.

lesson.bigIdea: An equation tells you how a quantity changes; a solution is a whole function that obeys that rule.
understand: An algebraic equation usually asks for a number. A differential equation asks for a function because its unknown appears together with derivatives. A proposed solution must work at every point of an interval, not just at the initial point.

Order counts the highest derivative. Linearity asks whether the unknown function and its derivatives appear only to the first power, without products between them. A coefficient such as t² is allowed in a linear equation; y², sin(y), and yy′ are not. An initial condition selects a trajectory from a family, when an appropriate uniqueness theorem applies.
lesson.why: Derivatives encode local information. Integrating reconstructs a function, introducing constants; an order-n regular linear IVP generally needs n initial values to determine them.
method: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
Find the highest derivative and inspect how the unknown enters.
To verify a candidate, calculate the required derivatives, substitute, and check the initial data separately.

example.prompt: Why does \(y=A\cos t+B\sin t\) solve \(y''+y=0\)?
example.explanation: Two derivatives change each sine/cosine term to its negative, so \(y''=-y\) for every A and B. If y(0)=2 and y′(0)=−1, those data give A=2 and B=−1. Satisfying the ODE gives a family; satisfying the data picks one member.

lesson.connection: This distinction between a rule and a trajectory returns in phase lines, linear superposition, and PDE modes.
checks: Does y(0)=1 alone prove that y=eᵗ solves y′=2y?
No. An initial value checks only one point. For eᵗ the derivative is eᵗ while the right side is 2eᵗ, so the differential equation fails.
Check the derivative as well as the initial value.
Why is t²y′+cos(t)y=t linear while y′+y²=t is nonlinear?
Coefficients may depend on t. The first equation is linear in y and y′; the second squares the unknown, which breaks linearity.
Ask which variable is being squared.

1.2.title: Integration and separation
goals: Keep equilibria and find the IVP interval
1.2.trap: Dividing by a function of y can discard constant solutions.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: What can be lost when solving y′=y(1−y) by dividing by y(1−y)?
hints: Set the state factor equal to zero first.
steps: The constant solutions y=0 and y=1. They must be listed separately because division assumes the denominator is nonzero.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Can y(0)=1 for y′=y² have a solution for all real times?
hints: Inspect the denominator of the IVP solution.
steps: No. Its unique trajectory is 1/(1−t), which blows up at t=1. Local uniqueness does not imply a global interval.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: A logarithmic substitution
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime=ty\ln|y|\).
hints: For y≠0 set u=ln|y|.
steps: \(u\prime=y\prime/y=tu\), so \(u=Ce^{t^2/2}\).
Exponentiate and choose the sign of y on its interval.
problems.check: C=0 includes y=±1. The original RHS is undefined at y=0.

problems.title: Projectile motion
problems.prompt: A projectile starts at ground level with vertical speed 100 m/s, horizontal speed 20 m/s, and gravity 10 m/s². Find flight time and range.
hints: Integrate vertical acceleration twice.
steps: The positive root of \(h(t)=0\) is t=20. Horizontal distance is 20t.
problems.check: At 20 seconds height is 0; air resistance is omitted as in the exercise.

problems.title: A separable IVP
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime=(1+\cos t)y\), \(y(0)=2\).
hints: Separate dy/y from dt.
steps: \(\ln|y|=t+\sin t+C\).
\(y=Ae^{t+\sin t}\); initial data gives A=2.
problems.check: Differentiation gives y′=(1+cos t)y; y(0)=2.

problems.title: Finite-time blow-up
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime=y^2/(t+1)\), \(y(0)=2\), and give its maximal interval.
hints: Integrate y⁻² and locate both types of singularities.
steps: On the interval containing 0, t>−1. The denominator vanishes when ln(t+1)=1/2.
problems.check: The interval must contain the initial point and stop at the first singularities.

problems.title: Keep the equilibria
problems.prompt: Solve \(y'=y(1-y)\), y(0)=1/2, and list the constant solutions of the ODE.
hints: Use partial fractions 1/[y(1−y)]=1/y+1/(1−y).
steps: Integration gives ln|y/(1−y)|=t+C. The data give C=0.
Solving gives y=eᵗ/(1+eᵗ). Before dividing, y=0 and y=1 must be recorded.
problems.check: The IVP solution stays in (0,1) for all real t and tends to 1 as t→∞.

lesson.bigIdea: Separation works when the time dependence and state dependence can be put on opposite sides.
understand: For y′=f(t)g(y), the change in y can be accumulated by integrating 1/g(y), while the time dependence is accumulated by integrating f(t). This does not always produce an explicit formula: an implicit relation can still describe a valid solution.

Before dividing by g(y), find its zeros. They may be constant solutions that the division discards. After solving an IVP, find the largest connected interval containing its initial time on which the original equation and your solution both make sense. Blow-up in a solution and an undefined coefficient are different reasons an interval can end.
lesson.why: The chain rule says \(\frac{d}{dt}\int^{y(t)}du/g(u)=y'/g(y)=f(t)\). Separation is this identity written in differential notation.
method: Check whether the RHS factors into a time function and a state function.
List any equilibrium solutions before dividing.
Integrate, impose the data, and state the interval containing the initial point.

example.explanation: Separating gives −1/y=t+C. The data fix C=−1, so y=1/(1−t). The solution becomes infinite at t=1; the IVP interval is (−∞,1). The equilibrium y=0 solves the same ODE but not these initial data.

lesson.connection: The same domain checks matter for integrating factors, Laplace IVPs, and nonlinear substitutions.
checks: What can be lost when solving y′=y(1−y) by dividing by y(1−y)?
The constant solutions y=0 and y=1. They must be listed separately because division assumes the denominator is nonzero.
Set the state factor equal to zero first.
Can y(0)=1 for y′=y² have a solution for all real times?
No. Its unique trajectory is 1/(1−t), which blows up at t=1. Local uniqueness does not imply a global interval.
Inspect the denominator of the IVP solution.

1.3.title: Slope fields
goals: Read the sign of a slope
1.3.trap: A vertical tangent can occur at a point where the explicit ODE is undefined.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: If y′=t−y, where are the horizontal field segments?
hints: A zero-slope locus need not be a trajectory.
steps: On y=t, because f(t,y)=0 there. This line is a zero-slope locus, not itself a solution: y=t has derivative 1 rather than 0.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Can two solutions of a smooth scalar IVP cross at the same (t,y)?
hints: Treat a crossing as a new initial condition.
steps: No, where local uniqueness applies. At a crossing they would share the same initial point, so uniqueness forces them to be the same local solution.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Circles in a slope field
problems.prompt: For \(y\prime=-t/y\), identify the solution through (0,2), its interval, and the slope at (1,1).
hints: Integrate ydy=−tdt.
steps: The positive branch is chosen by the initial data. It stops where y=0.
At (1,1), the field slope is −1.
problems.check: The point (1,1) is a field point, not on this particular circle.

problems.title: Read a nonautonomous field
problems.prompt: For y′=t−y, find the slopes at (0,1) and (2,1), the zero-slope line, and the solution with y(0)=1.
hints: Rewrite as y′+y=t and use an integrating factor.
steps: The slopes are −1 and +1; zero slopes occur on y=t.
A particular solution is t−1; the full solution is y=t−1+Ce⁻ᵗ. The data give C=2.
problems.check: The trajectory is not the zero-slope line; substitution gives y′=1−2e⁻ᵗ=t−y.

lesson.bigIdea: A slope field is a map of allowed tangent directions, not a collection of complete solutions.
understand: At a point (t,y), the equation y′=f(t,y) prescribes the slope of any solution passing through that point. A solution curve must remain tangent to these directions as it moves through the plane. Positive slopes mean increasing y, negative slopes mean decreasing y, and zero slopes mean an instant of horizontal motion.

If f depends only on y, the field repeats along each horizontal row. If f depends only on t, it repeats vertically. Neither a single arrow nor an isolated zero slope determines long-term behavior. At a singular point where f is undefined, the usual explicit ODE does not prescribe a tangent at all.
lesson.why: The derivative is the slope of the tangent line. Drawing many short tangent segments turns a local derivative rule into geometric information about trajectories.
method: Evaluate f at a few test points.
Locate zero-slope curves and undefined points.
Follow the directions from the initial point and check whether the qualitative behavior agrees with an analytic solution.

example.prompt: Compare \(y'=y\) with \(y'=-y\).
example.explanation: Both have a horizontal equilibrium at y=0. For y′=y, positive values increase and negative values decrease, moving away from zero. For y′=−y, the directions reverse and trajectories move toward zero. The field tells you stability before you integrate.

lesson.connection: Collapsing an autonomous slope field into a sign diagram gives the phase line in §1.7.
checks: If y′=t−y, where are the horizontal field segments?
On y=t, because f(t,y)=0 there. This line is a zero-slope locus, not itself a solution: y=t has derivative 1 rather than 0.
A zero-slope locus need not be a trajectory.
Can two solutions of a smooth scalar IVP cross at the same (t,y)?
No, where local uniqueness applies. At a crossing they would share the same initial point, so uniqueness forces them to be the same local solution.
Treat a crossing as a new initial condition.

1.4.title: Existence and uniqueness
goals: Check continuity near the initial point
Separate failure of a theorem from nonexistence
1.4.trap: A failed hypothesis does not by itself prove that a solution is absent.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: If fᵧ is not continuous, must uniqueness fail?
hints: Distinguish “not guaranteed” from “false.”
steps: No. The derivative criterion is sufficient, not necessary. Its failure removes this guarantee; uniqueness might still be proved in another way.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why is checking f(0,1) alone insufficient for the theorem?
hints: Think about nearby initial states.
steps: The theorem needs continuity on a region around the initial point so nearby states and times are controlled. A single function value says nothing about this local behavior.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: A singular coefficient
problems.prompt: Does the theorem guarantee a unique solution for \(y\prime=ty-y^2/t^2\), with y(0)=1 or y(3)=1?
hints: Inspect t=0 before differentiating with respect to y.
steps: The RHS is undefined at t=0, so the stated ODE has no classical solution there.
Near (3,1), f and \(f_y=t-2y/t^2\) are continuous.
problems.check: The local theorem does not guarantee a solution for every real t.

problems.title: Existence without uniqueness
hints: f is continuous near (1,0), but fy is unbounded.
steps: Existence is guaranteed by continuity. The derivative in y is \(1/(3t^2y^{2/3})\), undefined at y=0.
One solution is zero. Another for t≥1 is \([\frac23(1-1/t)]^{3/2}\), joined to zero for 0<t≤1. Both are differentiable at 1.
problems.check: The two solutions share the same initial value and satisfy the equation on a neighborhood of 1.

problems.title: A regularity interval
problems.prompt: For y′=y/(t−2), y(0)=1, give the theorem’s guarantee and solve the IVP on its coefficient interval.
hints: The singular coefficient occurs at t=2.
steps: f and fᵧ=1/(t−2) are continuous near (0,1), so the IVP is locally unique.
Separation gives y=C(t−2); y(0)=1 implies C=−1/2. The regular interval containing 0 is (−∞,2).
problems.check: The polynomial extends to 2, but the original explicit RHS is undefined there, so its stated ODE interval stops at 2.

lesson.bigIdea: Existence means a trajectory is available; uniqueness means the initial point chooses only one.
understand: For y′=f(t,y), continuity of f near the initial point gives local existence. Continuity of the partial derivative fᵧ is a convenient sufficient condition for local uniqueness. Check a neighborhood, not merely whether a formula happens to have a finite value at one point.

These are sufficient conditions. If a hypothesis fails, the theorem is silent; a separate argument is needed to decide what happens. A coefficient undefined at the initial point is more serious: the stated classical equation cannot hold there. Even excellent local behavior does not prevent a solution from blowing up at a later time.
lesson.why: Continuity permits constructing nearby trajectories; local Lipschitz control in y prevents two nearby trajectories from separating from identical initial data. A continuous fᵧ supplies that control.
method: Write the ODE explicitly as y′=f(t,y).
Locate singularities of f and fᵧ relative to the initial point.
State separately what is guaranteed about existence, uniqueness, and the interval.

example.prompt: Compare \(y'=\sqrt{|y|}\), y(0)=0, with y′=y, y(0)=0.
example.explanation: The first RHS is continuous but not locally Lipschitz at zero. Both the zero solution and a solution that stays zero until time a≥0 and then equals (t−a)²/4 satisfy the same data. For y′=y, fᵧ=1 is continuous; the zero solution is the only one.

lesson.connection: For regular linear IVPs, coefficient continuity is enough to obtain uniqueness on the coefficient interval.
checks: If fᵧ is not continuous, must uniqueness fail?
No. The derivative criterion is sufficient, not necessary. Its failure removes this guarantee; uniqueness might still be proved in another way.
Distinguish “not guaranteed” from “false.”
Why is checking f(0,1) alone insufficient for the theorem?
The theorem needs continuity on a region around the initial point so nearby states and times are controlled. A single function value says nothing about this local behavior.
Think about nearby initial states.

1.5.title: First-order linear equations
1.5.trap: Put the equation in standard form before choosing μ.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why is μ=e²ᵗ wrong for 2y′+2y=4?
hints: First identify p in y′+py=q.
steps: After dividing by 2, p=1, so a valid integrating factor is eᵗ. Choosing a factor from an unnormalized coefficient fails to match the product rule.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: In a tank, why is the salt-out rate not just the water-out rate?
hints: Check the units of each term.
steps: Water flow has units volume/time; multiply it by mass/volume concentration to get mass/time. The concentration is Y/V for a well-mixed tank.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Integrating factor IVP
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime+2y=1+t\), \(y(0)=0\).
hints: Multiply by e²ᵗ.
steps: Integration gives \(y=t/2+1/4+Ce^{-2t}\). The initial condition sets C=−1/4.

problems.title: Recognize a product derivative
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime+\frac{2t}{1+t^2}y=\frac{\cos t}{1+t^2}\), y(0)=1.
hints: The integrating factor is 1+t².
steps: \(((1+t^2)y)\prime=\cos t\).
problems.check: The denominator never vanishes on the real line.

problems.title: A tank with increasing volume
problems.prompt: Initially 10 kg salt in 100 L. Inflow: 10 L/min at 0.001 kg/L. Outflow: 5 L/min. Find salt mass Y(t) and when it is minimal (assume unlimited tank capacity).
hints: Volume is 100+5t; salt-out rate is 5Y/(100+5t).
Use μ=t+20.
steps: \(((t+20)Y)\prime=0.01(t+20)\). Integrate and use Y(0)=10.
problems.check: Y″=396/(t+20)³>0 for t≥0, confirming a minimum.

problems.title: A decaying forcing
problems.prompt: Solve y′+y=e⁻²ᵗ, y(0)=0.
hints: Multiply by eᵗ, then integrate e⁻ᵗ.
steps: (eᵗy)′=e⁻ᵗ, so eᵗy=−e⁻ᵗ+C.
At t=0, C=1.
problems.check: y(0)=0 and y′+y=e⁻²ᵗ. Both the forcing and the response decay.

lesson.bigIdea: An integrating factor turns a linear equation into a product derivative you can accumulate.
understand: In y′+p(t)y=q(t), the term p(t)y prevents directly integrating y′. Choose a multiplier μ whose own derivative is μp. The two terms then combine into the derivative of μy. This is the product rule used backward, not a formula to memorize without a reason.

In a mixing model, track amount rather than concentration first. Amount-in minus amount-out gives the derivative of salt mass. The outgoing concentration is current mass divided by current volume. Unequal flow rates make the volume time dependent, changing the coefficient of the linear equation.
lesson.why: Because \((\mu y)'=\mu y'+\mu'y\), choose \(\mu'=p\mu\), or \(\mu=e^{\int p\,dt}\). Then integrate \((\mu y)'=\mu q\).
method: Divide by the leading coefficient to get standard form.
Compute μ and write the product derivative explicitly.
Integrate, solve for y, impose initial data, and keep the model’s physical interval.

example.prompt: Why does \(y'+2y=4\) approach y=2?
example.explanation: The equilibrium balances the forcing and decay: 2y=4. Subtracting the equilibrium, w=y−2 satisfies w′=−2w. Every deviation decays exponentially, so the initial data affect only the transient.

lesson.connection: “Steady response plus transient” is the first-order version of particular plus homogeneous solutions in Chapter 2.
checks: Why is μ=e²ᵗ wrong for 2y′+2y=4?
After dividing by 2, p=1, so a valid integrating factor is eᵗ. Choosing a factor from an unnormalized coefficient fails to match the product rule.
First identify p in y′+py=q.
In a tank, why is the salt-out rate not just the water-out rate?
Water flow has units volume/time; multiply it by mass/volume concentration to get mass/time. The concentration is Y/V for a well-mixed tank.
Check the units of each term.

1.6.title: Exact equations and substitutions
goals: Use Bernoulli, homogeneous, and order reduction substitutions
1.6.trap: Keep lost equilibria when dividing; substitutions may restrict the domain.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why must a homogeneous substitution use y′=v+tv′, not just tv′?
hints: Differentiate the substitution before replacing anything.
steps: Since y=tv(t), both factors depend on t. The product rule contributes the extra v term; omitting it changes the ODE.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: When y′=p(y), why is y″=p dp/dy?
hints: There are two derivatives: one in t and one in y.
steps: By the chain rule, d[p(y(t))]/dt=(dp/dy)y′. Replace y′ by p to obtain p dp/dy.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Find a potential
hints: Integrate M with respect to t and match ψy to N.
steps: \(M_y=N_t=1\), so the equation is exact.
\(\psi=t^2+ty+g(y)\). Matching ψy=t+2y gives g=y².
The initial point fixes C=1.
problems.check: Differentiating this relation recovers the ODE wherever t+2y≠0.

problems.title: Bernoulli transformation
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime+y=t/y\).
hints: Multiply by 2y and set w=y².
steps: \(w\prime+2w=2t\).
An integrating factor gives \(w=t-1/2+Ce^{-2t}\).
problems.check: Use an interval with positive radicand. y=0 is not allowed in this original equation.

problems.title: Reduce the order
problems.prompt: Find the general solution of \(ty\prime\prime=y\prime\).
hints: Let v=y′.
steps: For t≠0, \(v\prime=v/t\), hence v=At.
Integrate again to obtain a quadratic plus a constant.
problems.check: These polynomials also satisfy the undivided equation at t=0.

problems.title: A nonlinear IVP
problems.prompt: Solve \((t+1)y\prime=y^2\), y(0)=1.
hints: Separate variables and find the singularity of the solution.
steps: The right endpoint occurs at ln(t+1)=1.
problems.check: Direct substitution verifies the equation and initial value.

problems.title: Exactness with initial data
hints: Integrate M in t, leaving an unknown function of y.
steps: Mᵧ=2t=Nₜ, so the form is exact. ψ=t²y+t+g(y).
Matching ψᵧ=t²+g′(y) to N=t²+2y gives g=y². The data set ψ=1.
problems.check: The differentiated implicit equation recovers the original; the local branch through (0,1) has nonzero N.

problems.title: Scale-invariant substitution
problems.prompt: Solve y′=1+y/t for t>0.
hints: Set y=tv, with y′=v+tv′.
steps: The substitution gives v+tv′=1+v, so v′=1/t.
Thus v=ln t+C and y=t(ln t+C).
problems.check: Differentiate to get y′=ln t+C+1=1+y/t.

problems.title: A repeated linear combination
problems.prompt: Solve y′=eʸ⁺²ᵗ−2.
hints: Let v=y+2t.
steps: v′=y′+2=eᵛ. Separation gives e⁻ᵛdv=dt.
−e⁻ᵛ=t+C₀, so e⁻ᵛ=C−t. Translate back to y.
problems.check: The condition C−t>0 is required by the logarithm and e⁻ᵛ.

problems.title: Missing independent variable
problems.prompt: Solve y″=(y′)² and include the constant solutions.
hints: Either set v=y′ or use y′=p(y).
steps: With v=y′, v′=v². Nonzero branches satisfy v=−1/(t+C₁).
Integrating gives y=−ln|t+C₁|+C₂. The excluded branch v=0 gives constant y.
problems.check: Use an interval not containing −C₁. The logarithmic branch has y″=(y′)².

problems.title: Another scale-invariant equation
problems.prompt: Solve y′=2y/t for t>0 using y=tv.
hints: Use v+tv′=2v.
steps: After cancellation, tv′=v. The nonzero branches give ln|v|=ln t+C, hence v=At.
The branch v=0 is included by A=0. Translate back with y=tv.
problems.check: Differentiating gives y′=2At=2y/t. This equation is also separable; more than one method can fit.

problems.title: A shifted state and a lost branch
problems.prompt: Solve y′=(y+t)²−1.
hints: Set v=y+t, so v′=v².
steps: For v≠0, separation gives −1/v=t+C. Thus y=−t−1/(t+C).
The excluded constant branch v=0 gives y=−t, which also satisfies the original equation.
problems.check: Use an interval avoiding −C for the rational branch; substitution verifies both families.

problems.title: Bernoulli with a quadratic nonlinearity
problems.prompt: Solve y′+y=y² and include constant branches.
hints: On y≠0 set w=1/y.
steps: The transformed equation is w′−w=−1, so w=1+Ceᵗ.
Taking the reciprocal gives y=1/(1+Ceᵗ). The lost branch y=0 is separate; C=0 already includes y=1.
problems.check: Restrict to intervals where 1+Ceᵗ is nonzero. Both equilibria 0 and 1 are accounted for.

problems.title: Reduce an equation missing y
problems.prompt: Find all solutions of y″+2y′=0.
hints: Set v=y′ and solve a first-order linear homogeneous equation.
steps: v′+2v=0 gives v=Ae⁻²ᵗ.
Integrating gives y=B−(A/2)e⁻²ᵗ; rename the arbitrary constants.
problems.check: The constant mode is retained and there are two independent constants.

problems.title: Use y as the intermediate variable
problems.prompt: Solve y″=−y(y′)² with y(0)=0,y′(0)=1, allowing an implicit answer.
hints: Use y′=p(y), so y″=p dp/dy.
steps: Near the initial point p≠0. The equation becomes dp/dy=−yp. Its solution with p(0)=1 is p=e⁻ʸ²/².
Thus dy/dt=e⁻ʸ²/², or dt=eʸ²/²dy. Integrate from the initial values to obtain the implicit relation.
problems.check: The integral is strictly increasing from −∞ to ∞, so it defines a unique real y for every real t. Differentiating the relation gives y′ and then the original ODE.

lesson.bigIdea: A useful substitution reveals a simpler variable hiding inside a complicated-looking equation.
understand: Exact equations describe level sets of a potential: Mdt+Ndy=dψ. On a simply connected region with the usual continuity assumptions, matching Mᵧ=Nₜ lets you reconstruct ψ. Solutions keep ψ constant, so the implicit curve is often the most natural answer.

The other tricks target structure. For a scale-invariant equation y′=F(y/t), set y=tv and remember y′=v+tv′. For a repeated combination y+at, substitute that combination. For Bernoulli y′+py=qyᵃ, use w=y¹⁻ᵃ to make it linear. If y is missing from a second-order equation use v=y′; if t is missing use y′=p(y) and y″=p dp/dy. Always revisit solutions excluded by division.
lesson.why: Each substitution changes the dependent variable so the chain rule turns a nonlinear or higher-order pattern into separation, a product derivative, or a first-order equation.
method: Classify the pattern before starting algebra.
Write the transformed derivative carefully.
Solve in the new variable, translate back, and check lost constants or forbidden values.

example.prompt: For \(y'+y=y^2\), why use w=1/y?
example.explanation: On a nonzero branch, multiply by −y⁻² to get w′−w=−1. This is linear: w=1+Ceᵗ and y=1/(1+Ceᵗ). The original equation also has y=0, which the reciprocal substitution excludes.

lesson.connection: Recognizing structure is more valuable than trying every method; this habit carries into forcing trials and eigenfunction selection.
checks: Why must a homogeneous substitution use y′=v+tv′, not just tv′?
Since y=tv(t), both factors depend on t. The product rule contributes the extra v term; omitting it changes the ODE.
Differentiate the substitution before replacing anything.
When y′=p(y), why is y″=p dp/dy?
By the chain rule, d[p(y(t))]/dt=(dp/dy)y′. Replace y′ by p to obtain p dp/dy.
There are two derivatives: one in t and one in y.

1.7.title: Autonomous equations and phase lines
1.7.trap: A zero derivative f′(y*) requires a sign analysis; the linear test is inconclusive.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Can a trajectory pass through an equilibrium where uniqueness holds?
hints: Apply uniqueness at the alleged crossing.
steps: No. Once it reaches that state it shares the data of the constant solution. Uniqueness forces it to agree locally, so it cannot cross through into another sign interval.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why can f′(y*)=0 not decide stability?
hints: Compare y′=y² with y′=−y³.
steps: The linear term vanishes. Higher-order terms may give attraction, repulsion, or one-sided behavior, so the actual signs of f on both sides are needed.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Read a phase line
problems.prompt: For \(y\prime=y^2-1\), classify equilibria and find the limit of the solution starting at y(0)=0.
hints: Factor (y−1)(y+1) and test three intervals.
steps: The sign is positive below −1, negative between −1 and 1, positive above 1.
Trajectories move toward −1 and away from 1. Starting at 0, the solution decreases toward −1.
problems.check: The explicit IVP solution is −tanh(t).

problems.title: Sustainable harvesting
problems.prompt: For \(P\prime=P(10-P)-h\), find the critical harvest and equilibria when h=16.
hints: Complete the square in P.
steps: At h=16, roots are 2 and 8. f′=10−2P gives unstable at 2 and stable at 8.
At h=25 the equilibria merge at 5; above 25 there are none.
problems.check: At critical harvest 5 is semistable; below the lower equilibrium the model predicts population collapse.

problems.title: A zero derivative test
problems.prompt: Classify y=0 for y′=−y³, and solve with y(0)=1.
hints: Test signs on either side instead of relying on f′(0).
steps: Below 0 the RHS is positive; above 0 it is negative, so both sides move toward 0.
Separating gives 1/(2y²)=t+C. With y(0)=1, choose the positive branch.
problems.check: Although f′(0)=0, the sign analysis proves attraction; the decay is algebraic rather than exponential.

lesson.bigIdea: A phase line predicts where a system moves without needing its explicit formula.
understand: For an autonomous scalar equation y′=f(y), the same state always has the same velocity. Zeros of f are equilibria. Between consecutive zeros, the sign of f is fixed if f is continuous and no other zero occurs, so arrows summarize whether the state moves up or down.

An equilibrium is attracting when arrows point toward it from both sides and repelling when they point away. The derivative test f′(y*)<0 or >0 is a shortcut for a simple root. If f′(y*)=0, inspect the signs directly. A parameter can create or destroy equilibria; in harvesting models, a stable and an unstable equilibrium can collide before disappearing.
lesson.why: Near a simple equilibrium, \(z=y-y_*\) approximately satisfies \(z'=f'(y_*)z\). Its exponential growth or decay explains the derivative test.
method: Solve f(y)=0.
Test a point in each sign interval and draw arrows.
Classify each equilibrium, then follow the interval containing the initial state.

example.prompt: What happens near y=0 for y′=y²?
example.explanation: The RHS is positive on both sides. A negative state moves upward toward zero, while a positive state moves upward away from zero. The zero equilibrium attracts on one side and repels on the other; calling it simply stable from f′(0)=0 would be wrong.

lesson.connection: Eigenvalues play a related role in linear systems: they measure growth and decay along particular directions.
checks: Can a trajectory pass through an equilibrium where uniqueness holds?
No. Once it reaches that state it shares the data of the constant solution. Uniqueness forces it to agree locally, so it cannot cross through into another sign interval.
Apply uniqueness at the alleged crossing.
Why can f′(y*)=0 not decide stability?
The linear term vanishes. Higher-order terms may give attraction, repulsion, or one-sided behavior, so the actual signs of f on both sides are needed.
Compare y′=y² with y′=−y³.

1.8.title: Numerical methods
goals: Distinguish step size from final time
1.8.trap: Euler uses the old point; Heun averages a predictor slope with the old slope.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does halving h typically halve Euler’s error at a fixed final time?
hints: Distinguish global O(h) from local O(h²).
steps: Approximately, in its asymptotic error regime for a smooth well-behaved IVP: Euler has first-order global accuracy. This is not an exact identity for every step size.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why must Heun evaluate the second slope at tₙ+h?
hints: Both the time and predicted state change.
steps: The second slope approximates the derivative at the end of the step, using the Euler-predicted state there. Reusing tₙ misses explicit time dependence.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Two Euler steps
problems.prompt: Use h=0.1 to estimate y(0.2) for \(y\prime=y+t\), y(0)=1.
hints: Apply the update twice, including the time in f.
steps: The exact solution is \(2e^t-t-1\), so at 0.2 it is about 1.24281.
problems.check: The error is about −0.02281.

problems.title: Predict and correct
problems.prompt: Use one Heun step of size 0.1 for \(y\prime=y+t\), y(0)=1.
hints: First predict with Euler, then average slopes.
steps: Old slope is 1. Predictor is 1.1. New slope at (0.1,1.1) is 1.2.
Corrected value is \(1+0.1(1+1.2)/2\).
problems.check: Exact value is about 1.11034, closer than Euler’s 1.1.

problems.title: One step, two methods
problems.prompt: For y′=−2y, y(0)=1, compute one step with h=0.25 using Euler and Heun, and compare with the exact value.
hints: The Euler predictor is 0.5; evaluate the second slope there.
steps: Euler gives 1+0.25(−2)=0.5.
Heun averages −2 and −1, giving 1+0.25(−3/2)=0.625.
The exact value is e⁻⁰⋅⁵≈0.60653.
problems.check: Heun is closer in this example; accuracy and numerical stability still depend on step size.

lesson.bigIdea: Numerical methods replace a curved trajectory by small, controlled local approximations.
understand: Euler follows the tangent at the current point for one step. It assumes the slope stays roughly constant during that step, so its local error comes from ignoring curvature. Smaller steps usually improve accuracy, but do not remove questions of stability or model singularities.

Improved Euler (Heun) first predicts an endpoint, evaluates a second slope there, then averages the starting and predicted slopes. It better accounts for changing slope. Compare methods at the same final time; the step count and step size must match that target. A numerical value is an approximation, not a new exact analytic solution.
lesson.why: Taylor expansion gives \(y(t+h)=y(t)+hy'(t)+O(h^2)\). Euler keeps the first two terms; accumulated global error is typically O(h) on a fixed interval under standard smoothness assumptions.
method: Record tₙ,yₙ and the step h.
For Euler use the old slope; for Heun compute a predictor before averaging.
Advance the time as well as the state, and compare with an exact result or a finer grid when possible.

example.prompt: Why can Euler destabilize a decaying solution?
example.explanation: For y′=−2y, Euler gives yₙ₊₁=(1−2h)yₙ. The exact solution decays for any positive time, but the discrete multiplier has magnitude greater than 1 when h>1. At h=0.75 it alternates sign while shrinking; at h=1.2 it alternates and grows.

lesson.connection: Stability of discretization is separate from stability of the differential equation; this matters again for numerical PDEs.
checks: Does halving h typically halve Euler’s error at a fixed final time?
Approximately, in its asymptotic error regime for a smooth well-behaved IVP: Euler has first-order global accuracy. This is not an exact identity for every step size.
Distinguish global O(h) from local O(h²).
