The second slope approximates the derivative at the end of the step, using the Euler-predicted state there. Reusing tₙ misses explicit time dependence.
Both the time and predicted state change.

2.1.title: Independence and the Wronskian
2.1.trap: W≡0 is decisive for solutions of the same regular homogeneous linear ODE; arbitrary functions require care.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: If one solution is twice another, what initial data are missing?
hints: Count directions, not symbols for constants.
steps: The two columns lie on one line, so they can represent only a one-dimensional set of value/slope pairs. Two coefficients do not create a second independent direction.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why is checking W at one regular point enough for a common linear ODE?
hints: Use the equation satisfied by W.
steps: Abel’s identity gives W(t)=W(t₀)exp(−∫p), with a never-zero exponential factor on the regular interval. A nonzero initial determinant cannot later vanish.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: A repeated-root pair
problems.prompt: Are \(e^{3t}\) and \(te^{3t}\) independent?
hints: Calculate a 2×2 determinant.
steps: This simplifies to e⁶ᵗ, which never vanishes.
problems.check: The extra t factor supplies the second solution for a repeated root.

problems.title: A redundant function
problems.prompt: Are \(e^{3t},2e^{3t},te^{3t}\) independent?
hints: Look for a constant linear relation before expanding a determinant.
steps: The second function is twice the first.
\(2e^{3t}-2e^{3t}+0\cdot te^{3t}=0\) gives a nontrivial coefficient relation (2,−1,0).
problems.check: Two proportional columns force the Wronskian determinant to vanish.

problems.title: Use the basis to fit data
problems.prompt: For y₁=eᵗ,y₂=e⁻ᵗ, compute W and find the combination with y(0)=3,y′(0)=1.
hints: At 0, solve A+B=3 and A−B=1.
steps: W=eᵗ(−e⁻ᵗ)−eᵗe⁻ᵗ=−2, so the pair is independent.
The initial equations give A=2,B=1.
problems.check: This is the unique solution of y″−y=0 with the supplied data.

lesson.bigIdea: A fundamental set supplies independent directions in the space of solutions.
understand: For a regular second-order homogeneous linear equation, the solution space has dimension two. Two independent solutions are enough to build every solution. Their values and slopes at a time form two vectors; the Wronskian is the determinant that tests whether those vectors span the possible initial data.

For solutions of the same regular homogeneous linear ODE on an interval, a Wronskian nonzero at one point stays nonzero, and a zero Wronskian implies dependence. For arbitrary unrelated functions, W≡0 need not imply dependence without extra assumptions. It is the common ODE and uniqueness that make the determinant test so strong.
lesson.why: The constants satisfy \(\begin{pmatrix}y_1&y_2\\y_1'&y_2'\end{pmatrix}\binom{C_1}{C_2}=\binom{y_0}{v_0}\). A nonzero determinant makes this initial-data system invertible.
method: Compute the derivatives and the Wronskian.
Check the regular coefficient interval.
Use the independent functions as a basis and solve for coefficients from the data.

example.prompt: Why can \(\cos t,\sin t\) match any y(0),y′(0)?
example.explanation: At t=0 their value/slope vectors are (1,0) and (0,1). They independently control displacement and velocity. At any t, W=cos²t+sin²t=1, so they remain a fundamental pair.

lesson.connection: A fundamental matrix is the system version of this same initial-data map.
checks: If one solution is twice another, what initial data are missing?
The two columns lie on one line, so they can represent only a one-dimensional set of value/slope pairs. Two coefficients do not create a second independent direction.
Count directions, not symbols for constants.
Why is checking W at one regular point enough for a common linear ODE?
Abel’s identity gives W(t)=W(t₀)exp(−∫p), with a never-zero exponential factor on the regular interval. A nonzero initial determinant cannot later vanish.
Use the equation satisfied by W.

2.2.title: Characteristic polynomials
goals: Handle real, complex, and repeated roots
2.2.formula: r=\alpha\pm i\beta\Rightarrow e^{\alpha t}(C_1\cos\beta t+C_2\sin\beta t)
2.2.trap: For a root of multiplicity m include t⁰ through tᵐ⁻¹.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why are eᵗ and 2eᵗ not enough for the double root r=1?
hints: A repeated root requires a new shape, not a new multiplier.
steps: They are proportional. The second independent mode is teᵗ, so the general family is (A+Bt)eᵗ.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What changes when roots move from −1±2i to +1±2i?
hints: Separate real and imaginary parts.
steps: The oscillation frequency remains 2, but the envelope changes from decay e⁻ᵗ to growth eᵗ. The equilibrium’s stability changes.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Characteristic roots
problems.prompt: Find the general solution of \(y\prime\prime+y\prime-6y=0\).
hints: Try y=eʳᵗ and factor the resulting polynomial.
steps: Each distinct real root supplies an exponential.
problems.check: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order of the equation.

problems.title: Characteristic roots
problems.prompt: Find the general solution of \(y^{(3)}-6y\prime\prime+9y\prime=0\).
hints: Try y=eʳᵗ and factor the resulting polynomial.
steps: Factor \(r(r-3)^2\).
The root 0 gives a constant; the repeated root 3 gives e³ᵗ and te³ᵗ.
problems.check: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order of the equation.

problems.title: Characteristic roots
problems.prompt: Find the general solution of \(y^{(4)}+2y\prime\prime+y=0\).
hints: Try y=eʳᵗ and factor the resulting polynomial.
steps: Both ±i have multiplicity 2.
problems.check: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order of the equation.

problems.title: A repeated-root IVP
hints: The characteristic polynomial is (r−1)².
steps: The family is y=(A+Bt)eᵗ.
The data give A=1 and A+B=0, so B=−1.
problems.check: The initial derivative is zero even though the solution is not constant.

lesson.bigIdea: Exponentials turn differentiation into multiplication, so constant-coefficient ODEs become polynomial algebra.
understand: If y=eʳᵗ, each derivative multiplies by r. Substitution produces the characteristic polynomial. Its roots supply independent modes. Real roots give exponential growth or decay; complex conjugate roots combine into real oscillations with an exponential envelope.

A repeated root does not give several copies of the same independent function. Multiplying by successive powers of t supplies the missing modes. For a real equation, conjugate pairs should be combined into real sine and cosine terms if real-valued solutions are desired. Count constants at the end: an order-n regular homogeneous equation needs n independent modes.
lesson.why: Since \(D^ke^{rt}=r^ke^{rt}\), \(P(D)e^{rt}=P(r)e^{rt}\). The root condition P(r)=0 removes the entire exponential factor.
method: Write and factor P(r).
Record each root and its multiplicity.
Translate roots into a real basis, then impose initial data if supplied.

example.prompt: How do the roots −2±3i describe a motion?
example.explanation: The real part −2 gives the envelope e⁻²ᵗ. The imaginary part 3 gives angular frequency 3, so the real solutions oscillate with period 2π/3 while their amplitude decays. Frequency and decay are different pieces of the roots.

lesson.connection: These roots become eigenvalues of the equivalent first-order system.
checks: Why are eᵗ and 2eᵗ not enough for the double root r=1?
They are proportional. The second independent mode is teᵗ, so the general family is (A+Bt)eᵗ.
A repeated root requires a new shape, not a new multiplier.
What changes when roots move from −1±2i to +1±2i?
The oscillation frequency remains 2, but the envelope changes from decay e⁻ᵗ to growth eᵗ. The equilibrium’s stability changes.
Separate real and imaginary parts.

2.3-2.4.title: Operators and inhomogeneous structure
goals: Combine a particular solution with the homogeneous family
2.3-2.4.trap: The sum of two solutions of L[y]=f has forcing 2f, not f.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Can there be more than one particular solution?
hints: Subtract two candidates.
steps: Yes. Any particular solution plus a homogeneous solution is another particular solution. “Particular” means one chosen solution, not a unique one.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why do you impose initial conditions after adding yₕ?
hints: Separate the forcing task from the initial-data task.
steps: The particular solution may have arbitrary initial values. The homogeneous family supplies the freedom needed to correct those values without changing the forcing.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Build the whole family
problems.prompt: Given \(y_p=t\) for \(y\prime\prime+y=t\), find all solutions and impose y(0)=2, y′(0)=0.
hints: Add the kernel of D²+1.
steps: \(y=t+A\cos t+B\sin t\).
The data give A=2 and 1+B=0.
problems.check: Applying D²+1 cancels the trigonometric terms and leaves t.

problems.title: One forcing, many solutions
problems.prompt: Solve y″−y=2 with y(0)=0,y′(0)=1.
hints: A constant particular solution works.
steps: Take yₚ=−2 and yₕ=Aeᵗ+Be⁻ᵗ.
The data give A+B=2,A−B=1, hence A=3/2,B=1/2.
problems.check: The constant handles the forcing while the exponential coefficients handle the initial data.

lesson.bigIdea: One particular solution handles the forcing; the homogeneous family supplies every remaining freedom.
understand: A linear differential operator is a rule that maps a function to a linear combination of its derivatives. Its kernel consists of the homogeneous solutions. If yₚ produces the required forcing f, adding any kernel element leaves that forcing unchanged.

More importantly, any two solutions to the same forcing differ by a homogeneous solution: subtract their equations. That proves the family y=yₚ+yₕ is complete. A particular solution need not satisfy the initial data; the homogeneous constants adjust the data afterward. Superposition of forced responses must keep track of their right-hand sides.
lesson.why: Linearity gives \(L[y_p+y_h]=L[y_p]+L[y_h]=f+0\), and \(L[y-y_p]=f-f=0\).
method: Write the operator L and identify its homogeneous basis.
Find any one particular solution of the forcing equation.
Add the homogeneous family and then solve for initial constants.

example.prompt: If L[y₁]=f and L[y₂]=f, what do their sum and difference satisfy?
example.explanation: The sum gives L[y₁+y₂]=2f. The difference gives L[y₁−y₂]=0. This is why adding two solutions to the same nonzero forcing usually does not solve the original problem, but subtracting them identifies the homogeneous freedom.

lesson.connection: Undetermined coefficients and variation of parameters are two different ways to find that one yₚ.
checks: Can there be more than one particular solution?
Yes. Any particular solution plus a homogeneous solution is another particular solution. “Particular” means one chosen solution, not a unique one.
Subtract two candidates.
Why do you impose initial conditions after adding yₕ?
The particular solution may have arbitrary initial values. The homogeneous family supplies the freedom needed to correct those values without changing the forcing.
Separate the forcing task from the initial-data task.

2.5.title: Undetermined coefficients
2.5.formula: y_p=t^s e^{\alpha t}P_m(t)\quad\text{with }s\text{ the root multiplicity}
2.5.trap: Include both sine and cosine in a trigonometric trial.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why include a constant term when forcing is t²?
hints: Closure under differentiation requires the lower powers.
steps: Differentiating a quadratic produces linear and constant terms. A general trial At²+Bt+C allows those contributions to cancel and match every power.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: When is undetermined coefficients a poor choice?
hints: Ask whether derivatives generate a finite closed family.
steps: For forcing such as ln t or sec t, repeated differentiation does not stay in a finite polynomial/exponential/trigonometric family. Variation of parameters is more broadly applicable.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: An exponential forcing
problems.prompt: Find a particular solution of \(y\prime+y=e^t\).
hints: Try Aeᵗ.
steps: \(y_p\prime+y_p=2Ae^t\). Matching coefficients gives A=1/2.
problems.check: Substitution yields exactly eᵗ. The general solution also contains Ce⁻ᵗ.

problems.title: Resonance with sine and cosine
problems.prompt: Find a particular solution of \(y\prime\prime+y=4\cos t-6\sin t\).
hints: Multiply the usual sine/cosine trial by t.
steps: Use \(y_p=t(A\cos t+B\sin t)\).
\((D^2+1)y_p=-2A\sin t+2B\cos t\). Hence A=3 and B=2.
problems.check: The factor t prevents overlap with the homogeneous solutions.

problems.title: Polynomial forcing
problems.prompt: Find a particular solution of y″+3y′+2y=t².
hints: Try At²+Bt+C.
steps: Matching t² gives 2A=1. Matching t gives 6A+2B=0. The constant gives 2A+3B+2C=0.
problems.check: Substitution cancels linear and constant terms, leaving exactly t².

lesson.bigIdea: Choose a trial family that differentiation keeps inside itself, then fit its coefficients.
understand: Polynomials, exponentials, and sine/cosine combinations have a useful closure property: differentiating does not introduce entirely new function types. That lets you guess a finite-dimensional family for the particular solution and reduce the equation to coefficient matching.

The main obstacle is overlap with the homogeneous family. If your trial is already killed by the operator, no coefficient can make it produce a nonzero forcing. Multiply by t enough times to leave the kernel. Even a pure sine forcing normally needs both sine and cosine in the trial because differentiation mixes them.
lesson.why: Differentiation acts as a linear map on these trial families. Coefficient matching solves that finite linear system. Resonance makes the naive map singular, and the extra t factors repair the trial.
method: Identify the forcing type and include every companion term.
Check for overlap with characteristic roots and multiply by the appropriate t power.
Substitute, match coefficients, and verify the particular result.

example.prompt: Why does \(y''+y=\cos t\) need a t factor?
example.explanation: Both cos t and sin t solve the homogeneous equation. A trial A cos t+B sin t produces zero under D²+1 for all A,B. The trial t(A cos t+B sin t) produces −2A sin t+2B cos t, which can match the forcing.

lesson.connection: The annihilator method explains the t-power correction in terms of root multiplicities.
checks: Why include a constant term when forcing is t²?
Differentiating a quadratic produces linear and constant terms. A general trial At²+Bt+C allows those contributions to cancel and match every power.
Closure under differentiation requires the lower powers.
When is undetermined coefficients a poor choice?
For forcing such as ln t or sec t, repeated differentiation does not stay in a finite polynomial/exponential/trigonometric family. Variation of parameters is more broadly applicable.
Ask whether derivatives generate a finite closed family.

2.6.title: Annihilators
goals: Use multiplicity to select a trial
2.6.trap: Applying an annihilator enlarges the solution space; match the original forcing afterward.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why does solving the enlarged homogeneous equation not finish the original problem?
hints: Substitute into P(D)y=f, not only AP(D)y=0.
steps: Applying an annihilator erased information about the forcing. The enlarged family includes functions whose original image is the wrong multiple or combination of forcing terms.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What annihilates a constant plus sin(2t)?
hints: Use a product for distinct forcing types.
steps: D(D²+4) is a valid annihilator. One factor kills the constant and the other kills the oscillation; constant-coefficient factors commute.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Build three annihilators
problems.prompt: Find annihilators for \(t^2+5t\), \(\sin3t\), and \(t^2e^t+\sin t\).
hints: Use a product for different forcing types.
steps: A degree-2 polynomial is killed by D³.
\(\sin3t\) is killed by D²+9.
\(t^2e^t\) is killed by (D−1)³ and sin t by D²+1. Constant-coefficient factors commute.
problems.check: These are valid minimal constant-coefficient annihilators for these functions.

problems.title: Choose the resonant trial
problems.prompt: Give the correct trial for \(y\prime\prime+y=\sin t\), then find a particular solution.
hints: The roots ±i already occur in the homogeneous operator.
steps: Trial: \(t(A\cos t+B\sin t)\).
The image under D²+1 is −2A sin t+2B cos t; take A=−1/2, B=0.
problems.check: The forcing annihilator is D²+1; the enlarged operator has roots ±i of multiplicity 2.

problems.title: Repeated resonance
problems.prompt: For y″−2y′+y=eᵗ, find an annihilator, the correct trial, and a particular solution.
hints: The original operator is already (D−1)².
steps: The forcing annihilator is D−1, making the enlarged operator (D−1)³. The new mode is t²eᵗ.
Use yₚ=At²eᵗ. Since (D−1)²[eᵗv]=eᵗv″, the output is 2Aeᵗ; A=1/2.
problems.check: The resonance correction is t², because the shared root has multiplicity two in the original operator.

lesson.bigIdea: An annihilator kills the forcing so you can see which new homogeneous modes a particular solution must use.
understand: A constant-coefficient differential operator can annihilate a forcing function: D³ kills a quadratic, D−a kills eᵃᵗ, and D²+ω² kills a sine/cosine pair. If P(D)y=f, applying an annihilator A(D) gives A(D)P(D)y=0.

The enlarged equation has more solutions than the original one. The new modes suggest a particular-solution trial, but you must substitute that trial into the original equation to determine coefficients. Shared roots between P and A increase multiplicity and explain resonance. Different forcing types can be handled with commuting operator factors.
lesson.why: If A(D)f=0 then \(A(D)P(D)y=0\). Factor multiplicities tell you the enlarged basis; remove the modes already belonging to the kernel of P(D).
method: Construct a forcing annihilator.
Factor the product operator and identify newly available modes.
Use only those new modes as a trial, and match the original forcing.

example.prompt: For \((D-1)y=e^t\), what is the new mode?
example.explanation: The forcing is annihilated by D−1, so the enlarged equation is (D−1)²y=0. Its modes are eᵗ and teᵗ. The first is already homogeneous for the original equation; the new mode teᵗ gives a particular solution.

lesson.connection: This is the operator explanation of the resonance adjustment in §2.5.
checks: Why does solving the enlarged homogeneous equation not finish the original problem?
Applying an annihilator erased information about the forcing. The enlarged family includes functions whose original image is the wrong multiple or combination of forcing terms.
Substitute into P(D)y=f, not only AP(D)y=0.
What annihilates a constant plus sin(2t)?
D(D²+4) is a valid annihilator. One factor kills the constant and the other kills the oscillation; constant-coefficient factors commute.
Use a product for distinct forcing types.

2.7.title: Variation of parameters
2.7.trap: These formulas assume the leading coefficient is 1.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why can integration constants in u₁,u₂ be omitted when finding one yₚ?
hints: Identify what those constants multiply.
steps: They only add constant multiples of y₁ and y₂, which already belong to yₕ. Omitting them chooses a convenient particular solution.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: For 2y″+y=f, can you use f unchanged in the standard formulas?
hints: The derivative coefficient must be one.
steps: No. Divide by 2 first; the normalized forcing is f/2 and the homogeneous equation is y″+y/2=0.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: A nonstandard forcing
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime\prime+y=\sec t\) on \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\).
hints: Choose cos t and sin t; their Wronskian is 1.
steps: \(u_1\prime=-\tan t\), so u₁=ln(cos t).
\(u_2\prime=1\), so u₂=t. Constants of integration are absorbed into yₕ.
problems.answer: y=C_1\cos t+C_2\sin t+\cos t\ln(\cos t)+t\sin t
problems.check: Differentiating twice gives y″+y=sec t on the stated interval.

problems.title: A forcing outside the trial families
problems.prompt: Find the general solution of y″=1/t for t>0 using variation of parameters with 1,t.
hints: The Wronskian is 1; u₁′=−1 and u₂′=1/t.
steps: Integrating gives u₁=−t,u₂=ln t, so yₚ=−t+t ln t.
Adding A+Bt absorbs the −t term into the homogeneous coefficient.
problems.check: Differentiate twice: y″=1/t. Integrals need not resemble a polynomial trial.

lesson.bigIdea: Let the homogeneous coefficients vary with time so they can respond to a general forcing.
understand: For a homogeneous pair y₁,y₂, a forced solution can be sought as u₁(t)y₁(t)+u₂(t)y₂(t). Allowing two variable coefficients creates extra freedom, so choose the convenient constraint u₁′y₁+u₂′y₂=0. Then the first derivative has no unwanted u′ terms.

The remaining equation is a 2×2 linear system for u₁′ and u₂′, with the Wronskian as determinant. Integrating gives the variable coefficients. Unlike undetermined coefficients, this method does not require a special forcing family, though the resulting integrals may not be elementary.
lesson.why: For \(y''+py'+qy=f\), solve \(u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0\), \(u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=f\). Cramer’s rule gives u₁′=−y₂f/W and u₂′=y₁f/W.
method: Normalize the leading coefficient to 1.
Choose a fundamental pair and compute W.
Integrate the two coefficient derivatives, construct yₚ, and add yₕ.

example.prompt: For \(y''=f(t)\), what does variation of parameters become?
example.explanation: Use y₁=1, y₂=t, W=1. Then u₁′=−tf(t), u₂′=f(t). Thus yₚ=−∫tf(t)dt+t∫f(t)dt. Differentiating twice returns f, just as integrating y″ twice would.

lesson.connection: The fundamental-matrix formula in §4.3 performs the same construction for systems.
checks: Why can integration constants in u₁,u₂ be omitted when finding one yₚ?
They only add constant multiples of y₁ and y₂, which already belong to yₕ. Omitting them chooses a convenient particular solution.
Identify what those constants multiply.
For 2y″+y=f, can you use f unchanged in the standard formulas?
No. Divide by 2 first; the normalized forcing is f/2 and the homogeneous equation is y″+y/2=0.
The derivative coefficient must be one.

2.8.title: Laplace transforms
2.8.trap: A time shift requires writing the function in terms of t−a.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why does forgetting −y(0) change the IVP solution?
hints: Derive the boundary term in integration by parts.
steps: It replaces the prescribed initial value by zero in the transformed derivative identity. The algebra might still look valid but it solves different initial data.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: How do you transform H(t−a)t for a>0?
hints: Rewrite the profile using elapsed time since the switch.
steps: Write t=(t−a)+a. Its transform is e⁻ᵃˢ(1/s²+a/s), because the delayed active profile is g(u)=u+a.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Transform an IVP
problems.prompt: Find Y(s) for \(y\prime+y=\sin t+6\), y(0)=2.
steps: Isolate Y by dividing by s+1.
problems.check: The initial value is included before solving for Y.

problems.title: Two inverse transforms
hints: Rewrite 4s+3 as 4(s−2)+11.
steps: Use \(\mathcal L[t^4]=24/s^5\) and an exponential shift.
The second transform splits into shifted cosine and sine transforms.
problems.check: The numerator shift is essential: the sine coefficient is 11, not 3.

problems.title: Laplace IVP solution
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime\prime-4y\prime+3y=e^{2t}\), y(0)=1, y′(0)=2.
hints: Factor s²−4s+3.
steps: Partial fractions give \(Y=1/(s-1)+1/(s-3)-1/(s-2)\).
problems.check: At 0, y=1 and y′=2; applying the operator to −e²ᵗ gives e²ᵗ.

problems.title: A switched forcing
problems.prompt: Solve y′+y=H(t−2), y(0)=0.
hints: The transformed equation is (s+1)Y=e⁻²ˢ/s.
steps: Invert with a delay of 2, including t−2 inside the exponential.
problems.check: The solution is zero before 2, continuous at 2, and satisfies the switched equation on each side. Its derivative jumps at the switching time.

lesson.bigIdea: The Laplace transform trades a time-domain IVP for an algebraic equation while carrying its initial data.
understand: The transform accumulates a function against the decaying weight e⁻ˢᵗ. For suitable functions this converts differentiation into multiplication by s plus correction terms from the initial values. Solve for Y(s), then identify its inverse as a combination of familiar transforms.

A delayed input needs more than attaching an exponential casually. The shift rule is L[H(t−a)g(t−a)]=e⁻ᵃˢG(s). Rewrite the active part in terms of t−a before using it. A transform solution for an IVP starts at t=0; a general time interval from a separation problem is a different kind of description.
lesson.why: Integration by parts yields \(\mathcal L[y']=sY-y(0)\). Repeating gives \(\mathcal L[y'']=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)\), so the initial data are built into the algebra.
method: Transform every derivative with its initial-value terms.
Isolate Y(s), factor denominators, and decompose if needed.
Invert using shifts and basic transforms, then check the data and equation.

example.prompt: What does \(e^{-2s}/s\) represent?
example.explanation: Since 1/s is the transform of the constant 1, the factor e⁻²ˢ delays that constant input until t=2. Its inverse is H(t−2), zero before 2 and one afterward. This is a time delay, not multiplication by e⁻²ᵗ.

lesson.connection: Laplace’s equation in Chapter 7 is a different object: a PDE for a steady spatial field, not this transform.
checks: Why does forgetting −y(0) change the IVP solution?
It replaces the prescribed initial value by zero in the transformed derivative identity. The algebra might still look valid but it solves different initial data.
Derive the boundary term in integration by parts.
How do you transform H(t−a)t for a>0?
Write t=(t−a)+a. Its transform is e⁻ᵃˢ(1/s²+a/s), because the delayed active profile is g(u)=u+a.
Rewrite the profile using elapsed time since the switch.

3.1.1.title: Undamped mechanical oscillations
3.1.1.trap: Resonance in an undamped oscillator produces a growing envelope.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does a zero initial displacement imply a zero solution?
hints: A second-order IVP has two initial data.
steps: Not if the initial velocity or forcing is nonzero. A spring at equilibrium can move away immediately when given a velocity.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why does resonance require a different trial?
hints: Compare the forcing frequency with ω₀.
steps: The forcing frequency matches a homogeneous mode, so the usual sinusoidal trial is annihilated by the ODE operator. A t factor creates the growing resonant response.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Forced oscillator IVP
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime\prime+4y=\cos t\), y(0)=0, y′(0)=0.
hints: The forcing frequency is not the natural frequency 2.
steps: Try A cos t: 3A=1, so yₚ=cos t/3.
\(y=C\cos2t+D\sin2t+\cos t/3\). Data give C=−1/3, D=0.
problems.check: Both initial conditions vanish; the forcing amplitude is reproduced.

problems.title: Undamped initial motion
problems.prompt: Solve 2y″+8y=0, y(0)=1,y′(0)=2, and find its period.
hints: Divide by mass to get angular frequency 2.
steps: y=A cos 2t+B sin 2t. The data give A=1,2B=2.
The period is 2π/2=π.
problems.check: The amplitude is √2; changing initial data would change amplitude and phase, not frequency.

lesson.bigIdea: An undamped spring converts energy between motion and displacement, producing sustained oscillation.
understand: Displacement from equilibrium creates a restoring force −ky. Newton’s law gives my″+ky=0. The frequency √(k/m) increases with stiffness and decreases with mass. Initial displacement and velocity determine the amplitude and phase, not the natural frequency in this linear model.

External forcing can excite a different frequency. Away from resonance, a sinusoidal particular solution has bounded amplitude determined by the frequency difference. At exact natural frequency with no damping, energy keeps being added in phase and the response can grow with time. This is why a bounded forcing need not create a bounded solution.
lesson.why: A root pair \(r=\pm i\sqrt{k/m}\) gives sine and cosine modes. The conserved energy \(E=\tfrac12m(y')^2+\tfrac12ky^2\) has derivative y′(my″+ky)=0.
method: Measure displacement from equilibrium and keep consistent units.
Compute ω₀ and the homogeneous oscillation.
For forcing, find a particular response and impose displacement and velocity data on the full solution.

example.prompt: What happens if the mass is quadrupled while k stays fixed?
example.explanation: The natural frequency is halved because it depends on the inverse square root of mass. The period doubles. This does not by itself determine the amplitude; amplitude still depends on the initial energy and any driving.

lesson.connection: Adding damping changes the energy balance and moves characteristic roots into the left half-plane.
checks: Does a zero initial displacement imply a zero solution?
Not if the initial velocity or forcing is nonzero. A spring at equilibrium can move away immediately when given a velocity.
A second-order IVP has two initial data.
Why does resonance require a different trial?
The forcing frequency matches a homogeneous mode, so the usual sinusoidal trial is annihilated by the ODE operator. A t factor creates the growing resonant response.
Compare the forcing frequency with ω₀.

3.1.2.title: Damped oscillations
goals: Use initial values and response amplitude
3.1.2.trap: Damping classification depends on the discriminant, not the damping coefficient alone.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Can underdamped motion have a positive damping coefficient?
hints: Compare γ to the critical value 2√(mk).
steps: Yes. Underdamped means γ²<4mk, not γ=0. It oscillates while losing energy.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What remains after a long time in a damped, sinusoidally driven oscillator?
hints: Separate homogeneous and particular parts.
steps: The transient decays for positive m,k,γ, leaving the bounded steady sinusoidal response. The forcing keeps supplying energy, so the motion need not vanish.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Critical damping IVP
problems.prompt: Solve \(y\prime\prime+2y\prime+y=0\), y(0)=0, y′(0)=1.
hints: There is a double root at −1.
problems.check: The repeated root requires the te⁻ᵗ term.

problems.title: Compare damping regimes
problems.prompt: Classify (m,γ,k)=(20,40,100), (25,50,25), (10,50,60), and give general solutions.
hints: Compute γ²−4mk for each set.
steps: First discriminant: −6400; roots −1±2i.
Second: 0; double root −1.
Third: 100; roots −2 and −3.
problems.check: Each pair of roots solves mr²+γr+k=0.

problems.title: Tune a suspension
problems.prompt: For mass 1500 kg and spring constant 40000 N/m, find the units and value of critical damping γ.
hints: Set γ²=4mk.
steps: Since γy′ is a force, γ has units N·s/m.
problems.check: The source prints Ns/m for k; a spring constant must have units N/m. This solution uses the physically consistent units.

problems.title: Underdamped data
hints: Roots are −1±2i.
steps: y=e⁻ᵗ(A cos2t+B sin2t).
At 0, A=1; the derivative gives −A+2B=0, so B=1/2.
problems.check: The envelope decays and the frequency is 2. The derivative condition fixes B after accounting for the envelope derivative.

lesson.bigIdea: Damping removes energy; its strength relative to mass and stiffness decides how the motion returns to equilibrium.
understand: The damping force −γy′ opposes motion. For m>0,k>0,γ>0, energy satisfies E′=−γ(y′)², so the unforced system loses energy. Underdamped motion oscillates with a decaying envelope, critical damping has a repeated real root, and overdamping has two real decay rates.

The discriminant γ²−4mk compares damping to inertia and stiffness. A large numerical value of γ alone says nothing without m and k. In a driven system, distinguish the decaying transient from the steady sinusoidal response. A forced amplitude peak depends on all three parameters and need not occur exactly at the undamped natural frequency.
lesson.why: The roots solve mr²+γr+k=0. Their real and imaginary parts encode decay and oscillation; the repeated-root case requires a t factor.
method: Compute the discriminant and characteristic roots.
Write the appropriate basis, including t for a repeated root.
Use the initial data; for driving, add a particular response and discuss transient versus steady behavior.

example.prompt: Why can too much damping slow the return?
example.explanation: For γ much larger than √(mk), one root is approximately −γ/m, but the other is approximately −k/γ. The fast transient dies quickly while the slow mode approaches zero more slowly as γ increases. Overdamped does not mean fastest.

lesson.connection: An RLC circuit has the same mathematics, with inductance, resistance, and reciprocal capacitance taking the roles of m,γ,k.
checks: Can underdamped motion have a positive damping coefficient?
Yes. Underdamped means γ²<4mk, not γ=0. It oscillates while losing energy.
Compare γ to the critical value 2√(mk).
What remains after a long time in a damped, sinusoidally driven oscillator?
The transient decays for positive m,k,γ, leaving the bounded steady sinusoidal response. The forcing keeps supplying energy, so the motion need not vanish.
Separate homogeneous and particular parts.

3.2.title: RC and RLC circuits
goals: Use complex amplitudes for sinusoidal forcing
3.2.trap: Charge Q and current I are different variables; I is the time derivative of Q.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Is Q(t)=I(t) in a circuit?
hints: Use the physical definition of current.
steps: No. Q is charge in coulombs and I=Q′ is current in amperes. Their units differ; one can be constant while the other is zero.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What does a phasor’s argument represent?
hints: Write A in polar form before multiplying by eⁱωᵗ.
steps: It is the phase shift of a sinusoidal response relative to the chosen input. Its magnitude gives the amplitude, while the real or imaginary part reconstructs the physical signal.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Charge an RC circuit
problems.prompt: R=2 Ω, C=0.5 F, E=10 V, Q(0)=0. Find Q(t) and I(t).
hints: Use RQ′+Q/C=E.
steps: The equation is 2Q′+2Q=10, or Q′+Q=5.
An integrating factor yields Q=5+Ae⁻ᵗ; A=−5.
Differentiate charge to obtain current.
problems.check: The final charge is CE=5 C; initial current E/R=5 A.

problems.title: RLC steady response
problems.prompt: Find steady-state charge for L=1, R=2, C=1, E(t)=cos(2t).
hints: Use Qₚ=Re(Ae²ⁱᵗ).
steps: The complex impedance for charge is −4+4i+1=−3+4i.
\(A=1/(-3+4i)=(-3-4i)/25\). Take the real part after multiplying by e²ⁱᵗ.
problems.check: Substitution in Q″+2Q′+Q gives cos(2t). Transients decay separately.

problems.title: Discharging capacitor
problems.prompt: For an RC circuit with R=4 Ω,C=0.25 F,E=0 and Q(0)=2 C, find Q and I.
hints: The time constant RC=1 s.
steps: The equation is 4Q′+4Q=0, so Q=2e⁻ᵗ.
Current is I=Q′=−2e⁻ᵗ.
problems.check: The negative current means charge leaves the capacitor under the chosen sign convention.

lesson.bigIdea: Circuit equations are balance laws: voltage drops add up, and current is the rate of change of charge.
understand: For a series circuit, Kirchhoff’s voltage law combines resistor drop RI, capacitor drop Q/C, and inductor drop LI′. With I=Q′, an RC circuit gives RQ′+Q/C=E(t), while an RLC circuit gives LQ″+RQ′+Q/C=E(t). Charge and current are related, but substituting one for the other without differentiating changes the model.

For sinusoidal driving, complex exponentials simplify the calculation because derivatives multiply by iω. Solve the complex amplitude algebra, then take the real part for cosine forcing or imaginary part for sine forcing. The complex phase records a timing shift between the input and response; the physical result is real.
lesson.why: Substituting \(Q_p=\Re(Ae^{i\omega t})\) gives \(A=[1/C-L\omega^2+iR\omega]^{-1}E_0\) for a cosine voltage of amplitude E₀.
method: Choose charge or current as the unknown and write the voltage balance.
Check units and initial conditions for that unknown.
Solve transients and steady driving separately; differentiate charge to obtain current.

example.prompt: Why does a charged RC circuit approach Q=CE₀ under constant voltage?
example.explanation: At steady state the current is zero, so the resistor drop vanishes and Q/C=E₀. Deviations from CE₀ decay with time constant RC. The capacitor charge levels off while the current goes to zero.

lesson.connection: The RLC and damped mass–spring equations share the same roots and forcing methods.
checks: Is Q(t)=I(t) in a circuit?
No. Q is charge in coulombs and I=Q′ is current in amperes. Their units differ; one can be constant while the other is zero.
Use the physical definition of current.
What does a phasor’s argument represent?
It is the phase shift of a sinusoidal response relative to the chosen input. Its magnitude gives the amplitude, while the real or imaginary part reconstructs the physical signal.
Write A in polar form before multiplying by eⁱωᵗ.

8.2.title: Linear algebra toolkit
8.2.trap: Eigenvectors must be nonzero; a singular matrix has no inverse.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does det A=0 mean Ax=b never has a solution?
hints: Check whether b lies in the column space.
steps: No. It means no unique inverse exists. Depending on b, a singular system can have no solutions or infinitely many; Ax=0 always has solutions.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why is the zero vector not an eigenvector?
hints: An eigenvector must describe a direction.
steps: It satisfies A0=λ0 for every λ, so it carries no information about a preserved direction or a specific eigenvalue. The definition requires v≠0.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Determinant and inverse
problems.prompt: Find det A and A⁻¹ for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\5&-4\end{pmatrix}\).
hints: Use ad−bc and the 2×2 inverse formula.
steps: Swap the diagonal entries, negate off-diagonals, divide by −33.
problems.check: Multiplying A by this inverse gives the identity.

problems.title: Solve a linear system
hints: Eliminate x₁ by subtracting twice the first equation from the second.
steps: The elimination gives −5x₂=−5, hence x₂=1.
Substitute into the first equation to get x₁=2.
problems.check: Both equations evaluate to their stated right sides.

problems.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
problems.prompt: Find eigenpairs of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\).
hints: Symmetric and antisymmetric vectors are useful.
steps: \(\det(A-\lambda I)=(3-\lambda)^2-4=(\lambda-5)(\lambda-1)\).
For λ=5 use (1,1); for λ=1 use (1,−1).

problems.title: Complex eigenpairs
problems.prompt: Find eigenpairs of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\).
hints: The characteristic polynomial is λ²+1.
steps: Roots are i and −i.
For λ=i take v=(1,i)ᵀ. For λ=−i take v=(1,−i)ᵀ.
problems.check: The conjugate eigenpairs correspond to rotation in real coordinates.

problems.title: A singular system
problems.prompt: For A=\(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), solve Ax=(3,6)ᵀ and decide whether Ax=(3,7)ᵀ is solvable.
hints: The second row is twice the first.
steps: det A=0. For (3,6), the second equation repeats the first: x₁+2x₂=3.
Write x₂=s,x₁=3−2s. For (3,7), the row relation would require 7=6, so it is inconsistent.
problems.check: A singular matrix can yield either infinitely many solutions or none, depending on the RHS.

problems.title: Inverse of a triangular matrix
problems.prompt: Find the inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\).
hints: Either row-reduce [A|I] or solve the entries in AB=I.
steps: The determinant is 6, so the inverse exists.
problems.check: Multiplication in either order gives the identity.

problems.title: A defective repeated eigenvalue
problems.prompt: Find eigenvalues and the eigenvector space of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\). Is A diagonalizable?
hints: Solve (A−2I)v=0.
steps: The characteristic polynomial is (λ−2)². The eigenvector equations require v₂=0, with v₁ free.
Only one independent eigenvector exists, so no two-vector eigenbasis is available.
problems.check: Algebraic multiplicity 2 differs from geometric multiplicity 1.

lesson.bigIdea: A matrix is a linear transformation; determinants, inverses, and eigenvectors answer different geometric questions about it.
understand: Matrix multiplication composes transformations, so its order matters. The determinant measures signed volume scaling: a zero determinant means some directions collapse and the transformation cannot be undone. For a square matrix, a nonzero determinant guarantees an inverse and one solution to Ax=b for every b.

Row reduction explains individual systems, including inconsistent or underdetermined ones. Eigenvectors identify directions the matrix stretches without turning: Av=λv for a nonzero v. Eigenvalues tell you the stretch, but multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial does not guarantee enough independent eigenvectors. That distinction becomes crucial when solving systems of differential equations.
lesson.why: Linear combinations are preserved: A(au+bv)=aAu+bAv. In a basis of independent eigenvectors, that action becomes separate scalar multiplications, making repeated applications and exponentials simpler.
method: For systems, row-reduce and check pivots and consistency.
For invertibility, compute determinant or identify full rank.
For eigenpairs, solve det(A−λI)=0 and then the nullspace of A−λI; keep only nonzero eigenvectors.

example.prompt: Why is a zero eigenvalue a sign of noninvertibility?
example.explanation: A nonzero eigenvector v with eigenvalue zero satisfies Av=0. The matrix maps both v and zero to the same result, so no inverse can recover which input was used. Conversely, a square singular matrix has a nontrivial nullspace.

lesson.connection: Eigenvectors decouple x′=Ax; the inverse fundamental matrix converts forcing into those coordinates.
checks: Does det A=0 mean Ax=b never has a solution?
No. It means no unique inverse exists. Depending on b, a singular system can have no solutions or infinitely many; Ax=0 always has solutions.
Check whether b lies in the column space.
Why is the zero vector not an eigenvector?
It satisfies A0=λ0 for every λ, so it carries no information about a preserved direction or a specific eigenvalue. The definition requires v≠0.
An eigenvector must describe a direction.

4.1-4.2.title: Systems: formulation and uniqueness
goals: Convert higher-order equations to first-order systems
4.1-4.2.trap: The state must include enough derivatives to reconstruct the original equation.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why is y alone not a sufficient state for a second-order IVP?
hints: Count the independent initial data.
steps: The derivative of the state needs y′, and the future depends on both y and y′. Two trajectories can pass through the same position with different velocities.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Must A(t) be invertible for x′=A(t)x to have a unique IVP solution?
hints: Distinguish a derivative rule from solving Ax=b.
steps: No. Continuity of A is enough for linear IVP uniqueness. Invertibility of A is not required; A=0 gives the unique constant trajectory for each initial state.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Convert and check uniqueness
problems.prompt: Write \(y\prime\prime+3y\prime+2y=\sin t\), y(0)=1, y′(0)=0 as a first-order IVP. Is it uniquely solvable?
hints: Let x₁=y and x₂=y′.
steps: The coefficients and forcing are continuous for all real t, so the linear IVP has a unique global solution.
problems.check: Recover y″ by differentiating x₁′=x₂.

problems.title: A third-order state
problems.prompt: Convert y‴+2y″−y=t, with y(0)=1,y′(0)=2,y″(0)=3, into a first-order system.
hints: Store y,y′,y″ as three state coordinates.
steps: Let x₁=y,x₂=y′,x₃=y″. Then x₁′=x₂,x₂′=x₃,x₃′=x₁−2x₃+t.
The initial vector is (1,2,3)ᵀ; all coefficients are continuous.
problems.check: Three state coordinates carry the three initial conditions of a third-order IVP.

lesson.bigIdea: A system tracks enough state variables to make the future derivative depend only on the present state and time.
understand: A higher-order scalar equation can be written as a first-order system by storing y and its successive derivatives. For a second-order equation the state (y,y′) records both position and velocity. Two states with the same position but different velocity can evolve differently, so position alone is not a complete state.

For x′=A(t)x+f(t), continuous matrix entries and forcing on an interval give a unique solution for each initial vector on that interval. A homogeneous fundamental matrix stores independent solution columns. Unlike scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication is order sensitive, so keep the state a column vector consistently.
lesson.why: The equation x₁′=x₂ identifies the velocity, and the final state derivative is supplied by the original highest-order equation. No information is lost if the full initial state is preserved.
method: Introduce one state variable for each derivative up to order n−1.
Write each derivative in terms of the state.
Transfer every initial condition to the initial vector and check coefficient regularity.

example.prompt: What state represents \(y''+4y=0\)?
example.explanation: Take x₁=y,x₂=y′. The system x₁′=x₂, x₂′=−4x₁ records how position and velocity interact. Its eigenvalues ±2i agree with the scalar characteristic roots, so both forms describe the same oscillation.

lesson.connection: This representation makes higher-order ODE methods and matrix system methods two views of the same object.
checks: Why is y alone not a sufficient state for a second-order IVP?
The derivative of the state needs y′, and the future depends on both y and y′. Two trajectories can pass through the same position with different velocities.
Count the independent initial data.
Must A(t) be invertible for x′=A(t)x to have a unique IVP solution?
No. Continuity of A is enough for linear IVP uniqueness. Invertibility of A is not required; A=0 gives the unique constant trajectory for each initial state.
Distinguish a derivative rule from solving Ax=b.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why does the definite integral begin at the initial time?
hints: Evaluate the formula at t₀.
steps: It vanishes at t=t₀, so the forcing contribution does not disturb the chosen initial vector. The homogeneous part supplies the initial state.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Can one replace Φ⁻¹f by fΦ⁻¹?
hints: Check dimensions before rearranging.
steps: Generally no: the first product is matrix times column vector, while the reversed expression may not even be defined. Matrix products also do not generally commute.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Diagonal forced system
problems.prompt: Solve x′=diag(1,−1)x+(eᵗ,1)ᵀ with x(0)=(0,0)ᵀ.
hints: Use Φ=diag(eᵗ,e⁻ᵗ) and integrate from 0 to t.
steps: The integral from 0 to t is (t,eᵗ−1)ᵀ.
Multiply by Φ.
problems.check: x₁′=x₁+eᵗ and x₂′=−x₂+1; initial vector is zero.

problems.title: Forcing a rotating system
problems.prompt: Solve x′=\(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\)x+(0,1)ᵀ, x(0)=0.
hints: Use Φ(t)=[[cos t,sin t],[−sin t,cos t]].
steps: Φ⁻¹f=(−sin t,cos t)ᵀ. Integrating from 0 gives (cos t−1,sin t)ᵀ.
Multiplying by Φ(t) gives (1−cos t,sin t)ᵀ.
problems.check: Its derivative is (sin t,cos t)ᵀ, equal to Ax+f, and its initial vector is zero.

lesson.bigIdea: A fundamental matrix supplies moving coordinates in which forcing can be integrated directly.
understand: The columns of Φ(t) are independent homogeneous solutions. Writing x=Φu describes the state in that evolving basis. When you differentiate, Φ′u already accounts for the unforced dynamics. The remaining motion Φu′ is exactly what the forcing must produce.

Thus u′=Φ⁻¹f. Integrate in these coordinates and transform back. Using a definite integral from the initial time automatically keeps the added forced contribution zero at that time. The order Φ⁻¹f matters; it converts the forcing vector into basis coordinates before accumulation.
lesson.why: Since Φ′=AΦ, substituting x=Φu into x′=Ax+f cancels AΦu and gives Φu′=f. Hence \(x(t)=\Phi(t)[\Phi(t_0)^{-1}x_0+\int_{t_0}^t\Phi(s)^{-1}f(s)ds]\).
method: Find an invertible fundamental matrix.
Convert forcing with Φ⁻¹(s) and integrate from t₀ to t.
Add the correct initial coordinates and multiply by Φ(t).

example.prompt: If A=0, what does the formula become?
example.explanation: A fundamental matrix is I, so the formula reduces to x=x₀+∫f(s)ds. Variation of parameters is ordinary integration expressed in the moving coordinates supplied by the homogeneous flow.

lesson.connection: This is the matrix form of scalar variation of parameters in §2.7.
checks: Why does the definite integral begin at the initial time?
It vanishes at t=t₀, so the forcing contribution does not disturb the chosen initial vector. The homogeneous part supplies the initial state.
Evaluate the formula at t₀.
Can one replace Φ⁻¹f by fΦ⁻¹?
Generally no: the first product is matrix times column vector, while the reversed expression may not even be defined. Matrix products also do not generally commute.
Check dimensions before rearranging.

4.4.title: Constant-coefficient systems
goals: Use Jordan form or matrix exponentials
4.4.trap: A repeated eigenvalue may not have a full eigenvector basis.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Are repeated eigenvalues always an obstacle to diagonalization?
hints: Compare algebraic and geometric multiplicity.
steps: No. The identity matrix has a repeated eigenvalue and every direction is an eigenvector. The issue is whether there are enough linearly independent eigenvectors.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: If all eigenvalues have negative real part, does a Jordan block prevent eventual decay?
hints: Compare tᵏ with e⁻ᵃᵗ for a>0.
steps: No. Polynomial factors times decaying exponentials still tend to zero. Jordan structure changes the transient shape but not asymptotic decay in this case.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: A symmetric system
problems.prompt: Solve \(v\prime=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}v\), v(0)=(3,5)ᵀ.
hints: Use eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,−1).
steps: Eigenvalues are 6 and 2.
Multiply each component by its exponential.
problems.check: At t=0 the vector is (3,5)ᵀ.

problems.title: A defective matrix
problems.prompt: Solve \(v\prime=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}v\), v(0)=(2,3)ᵀ.
hints: Write A=I+N with N²=0.
steps: \(e^{tA}=e^t(I+tN)=e^t\begin{pmatrix}1&2t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
Multiply by (2,3)ᵀ.
problems.check: The factor t appears because the repeated eigenvalue has a Jordan block.

problems.title: A rotation exponential
problems.prompt: Find \(e^{tA}\) for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\).
hints: Use A²=−I and split the exponential series into even and odd powers.
steps: Even powers sum to I cos t, odd powers to A sin t.
problems.check: At t=0 it is I and its derivative is A times itself.

problems.title: Two decay directions
problems.prompt: Solve x′=\(\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\)x, x(0)=(1,1)ᵀ.
hints: Solve the second component first and insert it into the first.
steps: x₂=e⁻ᵗ. Then x₁′+2x₁=e⁻ᵗ.
The family x₁=e⁻ᵗ+Ce⁻²ᵗ and x₁(0)=1 give C=0. Equivalently, (1,1)ᵀ is an eigenvector with λ=−1.
problems.check: The faster −2 mode has zero coefficient for this particular initial vector.

lesson.bigIdea: Eigenvectors identify independent motions; the matrix exponential evolves all of them together.
understand: If Av=λv, then eᵗλv solves x′=Ax. With a full basis of eigenvectors, decompose the initial vector into those directions and let each coefficient grow, decay, or oscillate according to its eigenvalue. Real parts determine exponential stability; imaginary parts describe oscillation.

A matrix can have repeated eigenvalues without enough eigenvectors. Then a Jordan block contributes polynomial factors in t, just as repeated scalar roots do. The matrix exponential is defined by its power series even when diagonalization fails. The identity e⁰ᴬ=I guarantees the initial value, and d(eᵗᴬ)/dt=Aeᵗᴬ guarantees the equation.
lesson.why: If A=PΛP⁻¹, then \(e^{tA}=Pe^{tΛ}P^{-1}\). For a block A=λI+N with Nᵐ=0, the nilpotent exponential terminates: \(e^{tA}=e^{λt}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}t^jN^j/j!\).
method: Find eigenvalues and independent eigenvectors.
Use an eigenvector basis if available; otherwise use a Jordan or direct exponential method.
Apply the evolution matrix to the initial vector and verify at t=0.

example.prompt: Why can eigenvalue 0 coexist with growth?
example.explanation: For A=[[0,1],[0,0]], both eigenvalues are zero, but A²=0 gives eᵗᴬ=I+tA. With initial vector (0,1), the solution is (t,1). A defective zero eigenvalue creates polynomial growth; eigenvalues alone need context at zero real part.

lesson.connection: Jordan blocks explain why repeated roots generate t factors throughout the course.
checks: Are repeated eigenvalues always an obstacle to diagonalization?
No. The identity matrix has a repeated eigenvalue and every direction is an eigenvector. The issue is whether there are enough linearly independent eigenvectors.
Compare algebraic and geometric multiplicity.
If all eigenvalues have negative real part, does a Jordan block prevent eventual decay?
No. Polynomial factors times decaying exponentials still tend to zero. Jordan structure changes the transient shape but not asymptotic decay in this case.
Compare tᵏ with e⁻ᵃᵗ for a>0.

5.1-5.2.title: Boundary values and solvability
goals: Check whether boundary equations are consistent
5.1-5.2.formula: \text{A linear BVP can have 0, 1, or infinitely many solutions.}
5.1-5.2.trap: Continuous coefficients do not ensure uniqueness for a BVP.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does the IVP uniqueness theorem guarantee a unique BVP with continuous coefficients?
hints: Compare endpoints with an initial value and slope.
steps: No. It controls initial data at one point. Constraints at different endpoints can be inconsistent or redundant even for smooth equations.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: If a forced linear BVP has one solution and a nonzero homogeneous solution with zero boundary data, what follows?
hints: Use particular plus homogeneous structure.
steps: It has infinitely many solutions: add any constant multiple of the homogeneous solution. Linearity preserves the forcing and endpoints.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Zero, one, or infinitely many
hints: Start with A cos x+B sin x.
steps: All three have A=0 from the left endpoint.
(a) gives 0=0, leaving B free. (b) gives 0=1, impossible. (c) gives B=1.
problems.check: Boundary equations, rather than the IVP theorem, determine solvability.

problems.title: A unique forced BVP
problems.prompt: Solve y″=2 on [0,1] with y(0)=0,y(1)=3.
hints: Integrate twice and apply endpoints.
steps: The family is y=x²+Ax+B. The left endpoint gives B=0.
The right endpoint gives 1+A=3, so A=2. The associated homogeneous zero-boundary problem has only y=0.
problems.check: Both endpoints and the equation are satisfied; the constants are uniquely determined.

lesson.bigIdea: A boundary problem constrains a trajectory at two locations, so compatible endpoint data become a separate question.
understand: An IVP selects a solution from values and derivatives at one point. A BVP selects a solution using conditions at different endpoints. Even when the coefficients are perfectly continuous, those endpoint constraints may be redundant or contradictory, giving infinitely many solutions or none.

For a linear BVP, first understand the associated homogeneous problem with homogeneous boundary conditions. If only the zero solution survives, the forced problem has a unique solution under the regular setting in the notes. If a nonzero homogeneous solution survives, a forced problem can have no solution or infinitely many. Adding that homogeneous solution to any one solution preserves both the equation and boundary data.
lesson.why: After writing a general ODE solution, the boundary conditions become a linear algebra problem for its constants. Rank and consistency determine how many members of the family satisfy the endpoints.
method: Solve the ODE family before imposing boundary data.
Translate endpoints into equations for the constants.
Check whether the equations determine, contradict, or leave free constants.

example.prompt: Why does y″+y=0, y(0)=y(π)=0 have infinitely many solutions?
example.explanation: The first condition sets the cosine coefficient to zero. The second is then automatically satisfied because sin π=0. It adds no new constraint on the sine coefficient; any multiple of sin x survives.

lesson.connection: Eigenvalue problems ask for parameter values where exactly this nontrivial homogeneous survival occurs.
checks: Does the IVP uniqueness theorem guarantee a unique BVP with continuous coefficients?
No. It controls initial data at one point. Constraints at different endpoints can be inconsistent or redundant even for smooth equations.
Compare endpoints with an initial value and slope.
If a forced linear BVP has one solution and a nonzero homogeneous solution with zero boundary data, what follows?
It has infinitely many solutions: add any constant multiple of the homogeneous solution. Linearity preserves the forcing and endpoints.
Use particular plus homogeneous structure.

5.3.title: Eigenvalue boundary problems
goals: Split positive, zero, and negative λ
Include a zero mode for Neumann conditions
5.3.trap: The identically zero function does not count as an eigenfunction.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why must the zero-function solution be excluded?
hints: A parameter is special only if a nontrivial shape survives.
steps: It satisfies the homogeneous equation and endpoints for every λ and carries no spatial mode. An eigenfunction is nonzero by definition.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why should λ=0 be checked even when positive-frequency formulas look complete?
hints: Solve y″=0 directly.
steps: It can produce a constant mode, particularly with Neumann conditions. Dividing by √λ or assuming a sine family can silently discard it.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Neumann eigenvalues
problems.prompt: Find all eigenpairs for y″+λy=0, y′(0)=0, y′(5)=0.
hints: Check λ=0 separately.
steps: For λ=k²>0, y=A cos kx+B sin kx. The first condition gives B=0 and the second sin(5k)=0.
For λ=0, y=A+Bx and B=0, leaving a nonzero constant.
For λ<0, hyperbolic solutions and both derivative conditions force the zero function.
problems.check: The n=0 eigenfunction is 1.

problems.title: Mixed boundary conditions
problems.prompt: Find eigenpairs for y″+λy=0, y′(0)=0, y(3)=0.
hints: Cos(3k)=0 replaces sin(3k)=0.
steps: For positive λ=k², the left condition removes the sine term.
\(\cos3k=0\Rightarrow k=(n+1/2)\pi/3\).
λ=0 and λ<0 yield only the zero solution.
problems.check: There is no constant mode because the right boundary is Dirichlet.

problems.title: Remove the first derivative
problems.prompt: Find eigenpairs of y″+2y′+λy=0, y(0)=0, y(π)=0.
hints: Set y=e⁻ˣz.
steps: Substitution gives z″+(λ−1)z=0 with the same zero endpoint conditions.
Nontrivial modes have λ−1=n², n≥1.
problems.check: The transformation shifts the eigenvalues by 1.

problems.title: Dirichlet on a different length
problems.prompt: Find eigenpairs of y″+λy=0, y(0)=y(2)=0.
hints: For λ=k²>0, require sin(2k)=0.
steps: The left condition removes the cosine coefficient; the right requires k=nπ/2,n≥1.
λ=0 and λ<0 only allow the zero function under these endpoints.
problems.check: The n=0 formula would produce the zero function and is excluded.

lesson.bigIdea: An eigenvalue is a parameter that permits a nonzero shape to satisfy homogeneous boundary constraints.
understand: The zero function satisfies a homogeneous linear boundary problem for every parameter, so it cannot distinguish eigenvalues. We look for nonzero functions. For y″+λy=0, positive, zero, and negative λ produce trigonometric, linear, and hyperbolic shapes, respectively; each case must be checked against the endpoints.

Dirichlet conditions usually select sine modes, Neumann conditions cosine modes including a constant zero mode, and mixed conditions half-integer frequencies. A first derivative term can shift the spectrum after a substitution. Do not use a memorized sine formula before examining the actual boundary types.
lesson.why: Endpoint constraints turn a continuous frequency parameter into discrete choices: for example sin(kL)=0 requires kL=nπ. Only those frequencies close up correctly at both endpoints.
method: Solve separately for λ>0, λ=0, and λ<0.
Apply homogeneous endpoint conditions and require a nonzero coefficient.
List the allowed λ and a corresponding nonzero eigenfunction, including indexing and any zero mode.

example.prompt: What changes between y(0)=y(L)=0 and y′(0)=y′(L)=0?
example.explanation: Dirichlet conditions remove constants and select sin(nπx/L), n≥1. Neumann conditions select cos(nπx/L), n≥1, but also allow the constant eigenfunction 1 at λ=0. That zero mode later preserves the mean in the insulated heat equation.

lesson.connection: These eigenfunctions become the spatial building blocks of Fourier series, heat flow, and waves.
checks: Why must the zero-function solution be excluded?
It satisfies the homogeneous equation and endpoints for every λ and carries no spatial mode. An eigenfunction is nonzero by definition.
A parameter is special only if a nontrivial shape survives.
Why should λ=0 be checked even when positive-frequency formulas look complete?
It can produce a constant mode, particularly with Neumann conditions. Dividing by √λ or assuming a sine family can silently discard it.
Solve y″=0 directly.

6.1.title: Orthogonal expansions
6.1.trap: An orthogonal basis need not be normalized.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Does orthogonal mean orthonormal?
hints: Check the denominator in the coefficient formula.
steps: No. Orthogonal means different basis elements have zero inner product. Orthonormal additionally means every element has norm 1.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What property characterizes the residual of an orthogonal projection?
hints: Take its inner product with any included basis element.
steps: The residual f−Pf is orthogonal to every basis function used in the projection. Those included coordinates have all been captured.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Project onto two functions
problems.prompt: On (0,π), project f(x)=1 onto the span of sin x and sin 2x.
hints: Use the integral inner product; both squared norms are π/2.
steps: \(\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=2\) and \(\int_0^\pi\sin2x\,dx=0\).
Divide by π/2 to get coefficients 4/π and 0.
problems.check: The residual is orthogonal to each of the two basis functions.

problems.title: Project onto constants and a cosine
problems.prompt: On (0,π), project f(x)=x onto span{1,cos x}.
hints: The squared norms are π and π/2.
steps: The constant coefficient is (1/π)∫x dx=π/2.
Integration by parts gives ∫₀ᵖⁱ x cos x dx=−2, so the cosine coefficient is −4/π.
problems.check: The residual has zero inner product with 1 and cos x; this is a projection, not an exact identity for x.

lesson.bigIdea: An orthogonal expansion separates a function into noninterfering components, just like perpendicular vector coordinates.
understand: For vectors, the dot product isolates a component along an orthogonal basis vector. For functions, an integral inner product does the same thing. Orthogonality means the cross terms vanish; it does not mean each function has length one.

Divide the inner product with a basis function by that function’s squared norm to get its coefficient. A finite expansion is a projection, generally an approximation. A complete infinite basis represents suitable functions in the appropriate convergence sense. At discontinuities, pointwise values require care; a function and its series need not agree at every isolated point.
lesson.why: If f=Σcₙφₙ and the φₙ are orthogonal, taking ⟨f,φₘ⟩ cancels all n≠m terms, leaving cₘ⟨φₘ,φₘ⟩.
method: Identify the interval, inner product, and basis.
Compute each numerator and squared norm.
Form the expansion or finite projection, and state its interpretation.

example.prompt: Why is the coefficient of sin x on (0,π) not simply ∫f sin x?
example.explanation: The squared norm is ∫sin²x dx=π/2, so the coefficient is (2/π)∫f sin x. If you use a unit-normalized basis instead, the denominator becomes 1; those are different conventions.

lesson.connection: Fourier coefficient formulas are projection formulas specialized to sine and cosine eigenfunctions.
checks: Does orthogonal mean orthonormal?
No. Orthogonal means different basis elements have zero inner product. Orthonormal additionally means every element has norm 1.
Check the denominator in the coefficient formula.
What property characterizes the residual of an orthogonal projection?
The residual f−Pf is orthogonal to every basis function used in the projection. Those included coordinates have all been captured.
Take its inner product with any included basis element.

6.2.title: Sturm–Liouville theory
6.2.trap: Use the weight r in both numerator and denominator of coefficient formulas.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: If the weight is r=x on [1,2], may you omit x in coefficient integrals?
hints: The norm denominator is weighted too.
steps: No. Orthogonality is with respect to ∫xfg, so omitting the weight uses the wrong coordinate geometry and generally yields wrong coefficients.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why do boundary conditions matter in the orthogonality argument?
hints: Track the endpoint terms rather than only the ODE.
steps: Integration by parts creates endpoint terms. The self-adjoint boundary conditions make those terms cancel; without that cancellation the usual orthogonality conclusion may fail.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Identify a weighted problem
problems.prompt: Write \((xy\prime)\prime+\lambda xy=0\) on [1,2], y(1)=y(2)=0 in Sturm–Liouville form; identify p,q,r and the inner product.
hints: Move the derivative term to the opposite side.
steps: \(-(xy\prime)\prime=\lambda xy\), so p=x, q=0, r=x.
Both p and r are positive on [1,2]. Distinct eigenfunctions are orthogonal under weight x.
problems.check: The interval avoids the singular endpoint x=0.

problems.title: A weighted projection
problems.prompt: With inner product ⟨f,g⟩=∫₁²x f(x)g(x)dx, project f(x)=x onto the constant function 1.
hints: Divide ∫x² by ∫x.
steps: The numerator is [x³/3]₁²=7/3. The squared norm is [x²/2]₁²=3/2.
The coefficient is (7/3)/(3/2)=14/9.
problems.check: The weighted residual integral ∫₁²x(x−14/9)dx is zero. The unweighted average would be 3/2, a different result.

lesson.bigIdea: Sturm–Liouville structure identifies the right weight and boundary conditions for an orthogonal eigenfunction basis.
understand: The form −(py′)′+qy=λry packages a differential operator with a weight r. With regularity, positivity of p and r, and suitable separated self-adjoint boundary conditions, its eigenfunctions for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal under the weighted inner product ∫fgr.

The weight is part of the geometry, not decoration. It appears in both coefficient numerator and norm denominator. Standard sine and cosine expansions are special cases with p=r=1 and q=0. More general coefficients create different spatial modes, but the idea of decomposing into orthogonal eigenfunctions remains the same.
lesson.why: Multiply two eigenvalue equations by the other eigenfunction and subtract. Integration by parts removes the derivative terms through the boundary conditions, leaving (λ−μ)∫ryλyμ=0.
method: Put the equation in Sturm–Liouville form and identify p,q,r.
Check interval regularity and boundary type.
Use the weighted inner product to project onto eigenfunctions.

example.prompt: How is y″+λy=0 a Sturm–Liouville problem?
example.explanation: Rewrite it as −y″=λy. Thus p=1,q=0,r=1. Dirichlet or Neumann separated endpoint conditions eliminate the boundary term in the orthogonality proof, leading to the usual sine or cosine basis.

lesson.connection: This theorem explains why separation-of-variables modes can be used as an expansion basis.
checks: If the weight is r=x on [1,2], may you omit x in coefficient integrals?
No. Orthogonality is with respect to ∫xfg, so omitting the weight uses the wrong coordinate geometry and generally yields wrong coefficients.
The norm denominator is weighted too.
Why do boundary conditions matter in the orthogonality argument?
Integration by parts creates endpoint terms. The self-adjoint boundary conditions make those terms cancel; without that cancellation the usual orthogonality conclusion may fail.
Track the endpoint terms rather than only the ODE.

6.3.title: Fourier sine series
goals: Integrate coefficients and interpret endpoint values
6.3.trap: A sine expansion is an odd extension; it takes value zero at the endpoints.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why is the sine series of 1 equal to 0 at x=0?
hints: Distinguish an open interval from its endpoints.
steps: Every sine term vanishes there. The odd extension jumps from −1 to +1, and its midpoint value is 0. The interior expansion is still correct.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: If L changes, can you keep sin(nx) as the basis?
hints: Fit the zero endpoints to the length.
steps: Only when L=π in this convention. The general basis is sin(nπx/L); both the frequency and coefficient normalization depend on L.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Sine expansion of a constant
problems.prompt: Find the Fourier sine series of f(x)=42 on (0,π).
hints: Integrate sin(nx) between 0 and π.
steps: Even coefficients vanish and odd coefficients are 168/(πn).
problems.check: At x=0 or π the series is 0, consistent with the odd extension’s jump averages.

problems.title: A linear function on (0,3)
problems.prompt: Find sine coefficients for f(x)=5−2x on (0,3).
hints: Integrate x sin(nπx/3) by parts.
steps: Let k=nπ/3. The integral is \([-(5-2x)\cos(kx)/k-2\sin(kx)/k^2]_0^3\).
It equals \((5+(-1)^n)/k\). Multiply by 2/3.
problems.check: This represents f in the open interval; the endpoint values of the sine series are 0.

problems.title: Sine coefficients of x
problems.prompt: Find the Fourier sine series for f(x)=x on (0,π).
hints: Integrate x sin(nx) by parts.
steps: Bₙ=(2/π)[−x cos(nx)/n+sin(nx)/n²]₀ᵖⁱ=2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n.
Insert these coefficients into ΣBₙ sin(nx).
problems.check: At x=π the series is 0, the midpoint value of the periodic odd extension’s jump, rather than the original endpoint value π.

lesson.bigIdea: A sine series builds an odd extension and is naturally matched to zero endpoint values.
understand: On (0,L), sine functions sin(nπx/L) form the spatial eigenmodes for homogeneous Dirichlet conditions. Their squared norms are L/2, giving the factor 2/L in each coefficient. You can expand a function that is not zero at the endpoints, but its sine extension then has jumps at those boundaries.

The odd extension determines the endpoint behavior. For piecewise smooth data, the series converges to the function at interior continuity points and to the average of the two one-sided values at a jump. Every sine term is zero at 0 and L, so a nonzero original endpoint value cannot be recovered there. This is a convergence issue, not an algebra error.
lesson.why: Orthogonality isolates \(B_n=(2/L)\int_0^Lf(x)\sin(n\pi x/L)dx\). The shape of the odd extension explains symmetry and jump behavior.
method: Use the actual interval length L.
Compute sine coefficients, exploiting symmetry or integration by parts.
State the interior expansion and check endpoint or jump interpretations separately.

example.prompt: Why does a constant have a nontrivial sine series?
example.explanation: A constant on (0,L) becomes positive on one half and negative on the reflected half under odd extension. That square-wave shape requires odd sine harmonics. The sine series is not trying to represent a constant on the entire reflected interval.

lesson.connection: The same Bₙ become initial-temperature coefficients in Dirichlet heat flow and displacement coefficients in fixed-end waves.
checks: Why is the sine series of 1 equal to 0 at x=0?
Every sine term vanishes there. The odd extension jumps from −1 to +1, and its midpoint value is 0. The interior expansion is still correct.
Distinguish an open interval from its endpoints.
If L changes, can you keep sin(nx) as the basis?
Only when L=π in this convention. The general basis is sin(nπx/L); both the frequency and coefficient normalization depend on L.
Fit the zero endpoints to the length.

6.4.title: Fourier cosine series
6.4.trap: These notes use A₀ as the constant term, not A₀/2.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why does A₀ use 1/L rather than 2/L in these notes?
hints: Compute ∫1² and ∫cos² separately.
steps: The constant function has squared norm L, while each positive-frequency cosine has squared norm L/2. Projection divides by the relevant norm.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: What extension corresponds to a cosine series?
hints: Compare cos(−x) with cos x.
steps: Even reflection about x=0, followed by periodic continuation of period 2L. Cosines are even, so the expansion shares that symmetry.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Cosine expansion of a constant
problems.prompt: Find the Fourier cosine series of f(x)=42 on (0,π).
hints: Compute the mean separately.
steps: For n≥1, the integral of cos(nx) is zero, so Aₙ=0.
problems.check: The cosine basis already includes the constant function.

problems.title: Cosine coefficients of a line
problems.prompt: Find the cosine expansion of f(x)=5−2x on (0,3).
hints: The mean is 2; use integration by parts for higher coefficients.
steps: With k=nπ/3, the cosine integral is \(-2[(-1)^n-1]/k^2\). Multiply by 2/3.
problems.check: At x=0 the sum is 5; at x=3 it is −1, matching the continuous even extension.

problems.title: Cosine coefficients of x
problems.prompt: Find the Fourier cosine series of f(x)=x on (0,π), using A₀ as the constant term.
hints: Compute the mean, then integrate x cos(nx).
steps: A₀=π/2. For n≥1, ∫x cos(nx)dx=[x sin(nx)/n+cos(nx)/n²].
Thus Aₙ=2[ (−1)ⁿ−1 ]/(πn²); even coefficients vanish.
problems.check: The series converges to the continuous even extension on [0,π], including both endpoints.

lesson.bigIdea: A cosine series builds an even extension and includes a separate constant mean.
understand: Cosine modes have zero derivative at the endpoints and match homogeneous Neumann conditions. Unlike the sine family, they include a constant zero-frequency mode. That mode has squared norm L; the nonconstant cosine modes have squared norm L/2, so their normalization factors differ.

These course notes write the series as A₀+ΣAₙcos(nπx/L), with A₀ equal to the mean. Some references write a₀/2 instead; mixing the conventions doubles or halves the constant term. The even extension often avoids a jump at the boundary in function values, though a derivative jump can remain.
lesson.why: Projection onto 1 gives \(A_0=(1/L)\int_0^Lf\). Projection onto the n≥1 cosine modes gives \(A_n=(2/L)\int_0^Lf\cos(n\pi x/L)dx\).
method: Write the convention for the constant term.
Compute the mean and higher cosine coefficients separately.
Interpret the even extension and use the correct interval length.

example.prompt: What is the cosine series of a constant c?
example.explanation: Its mean is c. Every higher cosine integral is zero, so the entire expansion is the single constant term. This is why a Neumann heat solution can retain a nonzero final temperature.

lesson.connection: In the insulated heat equation, every nonconstant cosine mode decays while the constant mean persists.

Compute ∫1² and ∫cos² separately.
