7.1.title: The heat equation
goals: Choose sine or cosine modes from boundary conditions
7.1.trap: Neumann problems retain the mean; homogeneous Dirichlet problems decay to zero.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why can an insulated rod approach a nonzero constant?
hints: Look for the constant eigenfunction.
steps: The Neumann zero mode has λ=0 and does not decay. It equals the initial mean, reflecting conservation of total heat in the insulated model.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: For endpoints held at 2 and 5, should the long-time limit be zero?
hints: Separate steady boundary data from the transient.
steps: No. The steady profile solves u″=0 with those values, so it is 2+3x/L. Only the deviation from that profile decays.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Dirichlet heat modes
problems.prompt: Solve uₜ=2uₓₓ on (0,π), u(0,t)=u(π,t)=0, u(x,0)=3sin x+sin 2x.
hints: Each sine mode evolves independently.
steps: For sin(nx), the spatial second derivative is −n² sin(nx).
The time equation is T′=−2n²T. Preserve the initial coefficients 3 and 1.
problems.check: At t=0 the initial profile is recovered; each mode satisfies the PDE and boundary conditions.

problems.title: Insulated endpoints
problems.prompt: Solve uₜ=uₓₓ on (0,π), uₓ(0,t)=uₓ(π,t)=0, u(x,0)=2+cos x.
hints: Use the constant mode and a cosine mode.
steps: The constant mode has eigenvalue 0 and stays fixed.
The cos x mode has eigenvalue 1 and decays as e⁻ᵗ.
problems.check: The preserved average is 2; the derivative at both endpoints is zero.

problems.title: Nonzero endpoint temperatures
problems.prompt: Solve uₜ=uₓₓ on 0<x<1 with u(0,t)=2,u(1,t)=5 and u(x,0)=2+3x+sin(πx).
hints: Subtract the steady linear profile before expanding.
steps: The steady profile is S=2+3x. Set v=u−S, giving homogeneous endpoint values and v(x,0)=sin(πx).
That single sine mode decays with rate π².
problems.check: Both endpoints stay fixed and the long-time limit is the steady linear profile, not zero.

lesson.bigIdea: Heat flow damps spatial variation: sharper modes disappear faster, while boundary conditions decide whether the mean survives.
understand: The heat equation uₜ=σuₓₓ links time change to spatial curvature. A temperature peak has negative curvature and cools; a trough has positive curvature and warms. Separating u=X(x)T(t) produces spatial eigenfunctions and decaying time factors. High frequencies have larger eigenvalues, so fine-scale variation fades fastest.

For zero-temperature endpoints use sine modes, which all decay. For insulated endpoints use cosine modes plus the constant zero mode; the average temperature is conserved. Nonzero fixed endpoint temperatures require a steady spatial profile plus a transient satisfying homogeneous boundary conditions. The initial coefficients come from the appropriate Fourier expansion.
lesson.why: If X″=−λX, substituting XT into uₜ=σuₓₓ gives T′=−σλT, hence \(T=e^{-σλt}\). Boundary conditions select λ and X.
method: Choose modes from the boundary conditions, subtracting a steady profile if necessary.
Expand the initial transient using those modes.
Multiply each coefficient by its decay factor and check the PDE and all data.

example.prompt: Why does sin(3x) decay faster than sin x on (0,π)?
example.explanation: Their eigenvalues are 9 and 1. The decay rates are 9σ and σ, respectively. The higher-frequency mode has stronger curvature for the same amplitude, so diffusion smooths it faster.

lesson.connection: Fourier coefficients describe the starting profile; the PDE prescribes how each coordinate evolves.
checks: Why can an insulated rod approach a nonzero constant?
The Neumann zero mode has λ=0 and does not decay. It equals the initial mean, reflecting conservation of total heat in the insulated model.
Look for the constant eigenfunction.

No. The steady profile solves u″=0 with those values, so it is 2+3x/L. Only the deviation from that profile decays.
Separate steady boundary data from the transient.

7.2.title: The wave equation
goals: Use both initial displacement and velocity
Divide velocity coefficients by modal frequency
7.2.trap: The sine-in-time coefficient is the velocity coefficient divided by ωₙ.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Why is the initial-velocity sine-time coefficient not just Gₙ?
hints: Differentiate the modal solution at t=0.
steps: Differentiating sin(ωₙt) introduces ωₙ. To reproduce velocity coefficient Gₙ at t=0, its amplitude must be Gₙ/ωₙ.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Does increasing wave speed c change the fixed-end spatial mode shapes?
hints: Separate X(x) from T(t).
steps: No. Boundary geometry determines the sine shapes. Increasing c changes their time frequencies and periods.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Wave equation with a linear profile
problems.prompt: Solve uₜₜ=9uₓₓ on (0,2), u(0,t)=u(2,t)=0, u(x,0)=x, uₜ(x,0)=0.
hints: Here c=3, L=2; expand x in a sine series.
steps: Zero initial velocity sets all sine-in-time coefficients to zero.
Attach cos(3nπt/2) to each spatial mode.
problems.check: The initial profile is recovered for 0<x<2. It disagrees with the right endpoint boundary, so the data do not define a continuous classical solution at that corner; use the Fourier/weak interpretation.

problems.title: Both wave initial conditions
problems.prompt: Solve uₜₜ=4uₓₓ on (0,π), zero endpoints, u(x,0)=sin x, uₜ(x,0)=4sin2x.
hints: Here c=2; modal frequencies are 2 and 4.
steps: The displacement excites n=1 with cos(2t).
The velocity excites n=2 with coefficient 4/ω₂=1 multiplying sin(4t).
problems.check: At t=0 the displacement is sin x and the time derivative is 4sin2x.

lesson.bigIdea: A wave mode oscillates in time rather than decaying; its two time coefficients encode displacement and velocity.
understand: For uₜₜ=c²uₓₓ, separation gives the same spatial eigenfunctions as the corresponding boundary eigenproblem, but T″+c²λT=0. Each mode has angular frequency c√λ. Initial displacement determines its cosine-in-time coefficient, and initial velocity determines its sine-in-time coefficient after division by that frequency.

Fixed ends use sine modes. In the ideal undamped model there is no exponential decay: energy moves between kinetic and deformation energy. Endpoint-incompatible initial data can still be interpreted using Fourier or weak solutions, but do not define a smooth classical solution at an inconsistent initial corner.
lesson.why: Write \(T_n=B_n\cos(\omega_nt)+C_n\sin(\omega_nt)\). At t=0, Tₙ=Bₙ and Tₙ′=ωₙCₙ, so a velocity coefficient Gₙ requires Cₙ=Gₙ/ωₙ.
method: Determine spatial eigenmodes from the endpoints.
Expand both initial displacement and initial velocity.
Attach cosine and sine time factors with the correct frequency normalization.

example.prompt: For u(x,0)=0 and uₜ(x,0)=sin x on (0,π), what is the motion?
example.explanation: Only the n=1 mode is excited. Its angular frequency is c. Zero displacement removes the cosine-time term; the velocity condition sets the sine-time amplitude to 1/c.

lesson.connection: Compare with heat flow: the same spatial basis evolves by decaying exponentials in heat, but oscillatory functions in waves.
checks: Why is the initial-velocity sine-time coefficient not just Gₙ?
Differentiating sin(ωₙt) introduces ωₙ. To reproduce velocity coefficient Gₙ at t=0, its amplitude must be Gₙ/ωₙ.
Differentiate the modal solution at t=0.
Does increasing wave speed c change the fixed-end spatial mode shapes?
No. Boundary geometry determines the sine shapes. Increasing c changes their time frequencies and periods.
Separate X(x) from T(t).

7.3.title: Laplace’s equation
goals: Normalize hyperbolic factors at the forced edge
7.3.trap: One coordinate has oscillatory modes; the other has hyperbolic modes.

problems.title: Explain the idea
problems.prompt: Is solving Laplace’s equation the same as taking a Laplace transform?
hints: Compare the roles of x,y versus t,s.
steps: No. Laplace’s equation is a steady spatial PDE, Δu=0. A Laplace transform is an integral technique for time-domain functions and IVPs.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: Test a misconception
problems.prompt: Why divide a mode by sinh(nH) when the forced edge is y=H?
hints: Evaluate the proposed mode on the forced edge.
steps: It makes the hyperbolic factor equal to 1 at that edge, so the Fourier coefficient there is reproduced exactly. Without this normalization the boundary amplitude is wrong.
problems.check: A complete response explains why, rather than naming a formula.

problems.title: One nonzero edge
problems.prompt: On 0<x<π, 0<y<1 solve Δu=0 with u(0,y)=u(π,y)=u(x,0)=0 and u(x,1)=sin(2x).
hints: Choose X=sin(2x); then Y″−4Y=0.
steps: The bottom boundary removes the cosh term, so Y=B sinh(2y).
The top boundary gives B=1/sinh 2.
problems.check: uₓₓ=−4u and uᵧᵧ=4u; all four edges match.

problems.title: A second harmonic edge
problems.prompt: Solve Δu=0 on 0<x<π,0<y<2 with zero left, right, and bottom edges and u(x,2)=3sin x+sin3x.
hints: Each top-edge sine component gets its own normalized hyperbolic factor.
steps: For n=1 use sin x sinh y/sinh2. For n=3 use sin3x sinh3y/sinh6.
Multiply by the top-edge coefficients and add the modes.
problems.check: Each mode is harmonic and the normalization gives the exact top-edge values.

lesson.bigIdea: Laplace’s equation describes a steady spatial balance, determined by boundary values rather than initial time data.
understand: At steady temperature, the time derivative in the heat equation is zero, leaving uₓₓ+uᵧᵧ=0. Curvature in one direction must balance curvature in the other. There is no time variable to evolve, and the boundary data specify the field inside a region.

On a rectangle, choose an eigenfunction family in the coordinate with two homogeneous edge conditions. If that coordinate supplies sine modes with X″=−λX, the other factor must satisfy Y″=+λY, giving hyperbolic functions. Normalize that factor so it equals the required coefficient at the nonzero edge. If several edges are nonzero, split into subproblems and superpose.
lesson.why: Substitution of u=XY gives X″/X+Y″/Y=0. Choosing X″=−λX forces Y″=λY, so trigonometric and hyperbolic behavior must occur together.
method: Identify which pair of homogeneous edges determines the spatial eigenbasis.
Solve the hyperbolic factor with the remaining homogeneous edge.
Expand the forced edge, normalize each mode, and combine by linearity.

example.prompt: Why is sin(nx)sinh(ny) harmonic?
example.explanation: Its x second derivative is −n² times itself, while its y second derivative is +n² times itself. The two cancel. A sine in both coordinates would give two negative terms and would not solve Laplace’s equation.

lesson.connection: This uses the same boundary eigenfunctions and Fourier projections as heat and wave equations, with a different evolution variable.
